## Ordinary least squares, a reminder {.center .pitfall-divider background-gradient="linear-gradient(160deg, #f7f4ef 0%, #d6e2f5 100%)"}

## The formula is the model {#sec-lm-formula}

In R the same line is `response ~ predictors`. Read `~` as "described by".

::: {.incremental}
- `+` adds a term. `-` or `-1` drops one, including the intercept.

- `:` is an interaction. `*` is the interaction and the main effects. `^n` adds interactions up to degree $n$.

- `I()` is arithmetic. `age^2` in a formula is not $age^2$. The square is `I(age^2)`.
:::


`y ~ 1` is the [null model]{.mark}: the mean, and no covariate. One mixed formula example is `Income ~ age^2 + I(weight/height^2) + gender`.

::: {.notes}
Step fragments: `+`/`-`, `:`/`*`/`^n`, `I()` for arithmetic. `y~1` is intercept-only. `age^2` in a formula is not squared age—`I(age^2)` is. Mixed example at the bottom is one sentence.
:::

## One row, then every row {#sec-lm-matrix}

For one observation,

$$
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_{p-1} x_{i,p-1} + \varepsilon_i.
$$

Stacked, that is $\mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$. The first column of $\mathbf{X}$ is 1 when the model has an intercept. Least squares chooses $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ to minimise the sum of squared vertical residuals. The fitted values are $\hat{\mathbf{Y}} = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{Y}$, and $\mathbf{H}$ is the hat matrix.

![](figures/generated/sketch-nongauss-a-matrix.png){.sketch-sm fig-alt="Block picture of Y equals X beta plus epsilon: a green column Y, a grey matrix X whose first column of ones is yellow, a red column beta, and a grey column epsilon, with one blue row i across Y and X." fig-align="center"}

::: {.notes}
Display $Y_i=\beta_0+\cdots+\varepsilon_i$, then $\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}$. $\hat{\mathbf{Y}}=\mathbf{H}\mathbf{Y}$ introduces the hat matrix for leverage later.
:::

## Ordinary least squares is BLUE {#sec-gauss-markov}

The [Gauss–Markov theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%E2%80%93Markov_theorem): if $\mathbb{E}(\varepsilon_i) = 0$, the $\varepsilon_i$ are uncorrelated, each has the same finite variance $\sigma^2$, and $\mathbf{X}$ has full column rank, then

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = (\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{Y}
$$

has the smallest variance among [linear unbiased]{.mark} estimators. The errors do not have to be Gaussian for that result. Gauss used normality. Markov removed it.

If, in addition, the $\varepsilon_i$ are independent and Gaussian, that same $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ is the maximum-likelihood estimator. The $t$ tests and the $F$ test on the printout use this extra assumption. If the variances differ or the errors are correlated, the corresponding estimator is generalised least squares, which is the [Welch case](#sec-ols-replacements) when the variance is a group.

::: {.notes}
Gauss–Markov needs zero mean, uncorrelated equal-variance errors, full-rank $\mathbf{X}$—not Gaussian errors for BLUE. Gaussianity enters for MLE and for $t$/ $F$ on the printout. GLS is named when variance differs.

**Going further.** Gauss–Markov restricts the competition to linear unbiased estimators: a biased estimator such as ridge regression, or the James–Stein estimator when $p \ge 3$, can have a smaller mean squared error. Without Gaussian errors, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ is still asymptotically normal, with covariance $\sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{-1}$, provided no single row of $\mathbf{X}$ dominates (the Lindeberg condition, $\max_i h_{ii} \to 0$); the $t$ and $F$ tests are then approximately valid for large $n$. With Gaussian errors the result strengthens to minimum variance among all unbiased estimators, since OLS attains the Cramér–Rao bound.
:::

## A coefficient is a $t$ {#sec-lm-t}

`summary(lm)` tests each coefficient against 0. The statistic is the estimate divided by its standard error. [Angelino and Marcone](https://www.sib.swiss/training/course/20260907_ADDMG) note that this test assumes Gaussian residuals. It is the interesting test for a slope. It is rarely the question for the intercept.

In a model with several covariates, each line is the test of that coefficient **with the other terms already in the model**. [Mahanty](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/interpreting-linear-model-output-r-anil-mahanty/) (9 January 2018) maps the same printout. Two of his readings do not travel: multiple $R$ is not a count of points on the line, and a small $p$ is not a verdict that the model fits.

::: {.notes}
Each `summary(lm)` line tests that coefficient with others already in. Mahanty's two warnings: multiple $R$ is not a point count; small $p$ is not goodness of fit. Intercept $t$ is rarely the scientific question.

**Going further.** Under independent Gaussian errors, $(\hat{\beta}_k - \beta_k)/\mathrm{SE}(\hat{\beta}_k)$ has an exact $t_{n - p}$ distribution because $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ and $\hat{\sigma}^2$ are independent and $(n - p)\hat{\sigma}^2/\sigma^2 \sim \chi^2_{n - p}$ (Cochran's theorem). Without normality the ratio is asymptotically standard normal under the conditions of the previous slide. $\mathrm{SE}(\hat{\beta}_k) = \hat{\sigma}\sqrt{\{(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\}_{kk}}$ grows when $x_k$ is correlated with the other columns, by the variance inflation factor $1/(1 - R_k^2)$.
:::

## The $F$ test compares two nested models {#sec-lm-f}

The $F$ statistic on the same printout compares the fitted model with the [intercept-only model]{.mark}. The statistic is the drop in the residual sum of squares, per extra parameter, divided by the remaining residual mean square:

$$
\frac{\{\mathrm{SS}(\mathrm{mean}) - \mathrm{SS}(\mathrm{fit})\}/(p_{\mathrm{fit}} - p_{\mathrm{mean}})}{\mathrm{SS}(\mathrm{fit})/(n - p_{\mathrm{fit}})}.
$$

With a single slope, this $F$ matches the $t$ test of that slope. With several slopes, every coefficient can be quiet and the $F$ test can still reject. $R^2$ is the share of the variance of $Y$ that the fit captures. Adjusted $R^2$ charges a cost for each extra term. The residual degrees of freedom are $n$ minus the number of estimated parameters.

::: {.notes}
Read the $F$ ratio formula once; with one slope it matches slope $t$. Several quiet slopes can still yield a significant $F$. $R^2$ and adjusted $R^2$ definitions are on the slide—df is $n$ minus parameter count.

**Going further.** Under Gaussian errors and the null that the extra $q = p_{\mathrm{fit}} - p_{\mathrm{mean}}$ coefficients are zero, the ratio is exactly $F_{q,\, n - p_{\mathrm{fit}}}$. With $q = 1$ it equals the square of the $t$ statistic of that coefficient. It is a monotone function of the likelihood-ratio statistic for Gaussian models, so it is the small-sample version of the deviance test used for GLMs. $R^2$ never decreases when a term is added; adjusted $R^2 = 1 - (1 - R^2)(n - 1)/(n - p)$ can.
:::

## Four plots, then two more {#sec-lm-plot}

`plot()` on an `lm` draws four checks by default, `which = c(1, 2, 3, 5)` ([`plot.lm`](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/stats/versions/3.6.2/topics/plot.lm)). [Tay](https://www.r-bloggers.com/2019/11/the-hidden-diagnostic-plots-for-the-lm-object/) adds the two it hides, both on [Cook's distance]{.mark}: `which = 4` and `which = 6`.

The next six slides pair a fit that respects the assumption with one that does not. Illustrative draws, seed `20261005`.

::: {.notes}
Default `plot(lm)` is which 1, 2, 3, 5; Tay (14 November 2019) adds Cook's distance by row (4) and Cook's distance against leverage (6), and treats a Cook's distance above 1 as a point to inspect. The six figures that follow use the same simulated fits.
:::

## Residuals against the fitted values

![Two residual-versus-fitted plots. Left: a flat cloud around zero. Right: a U-shape from fitting a straight line to a quadratic.](figures/generated/lm-resid-fitted.png){fig-alt="Left, residuals from a straight-line fit sit in a flat band around zero. Right, residuals from a straight line fitted to a quadratic curve form a U." width="96%"}

A flat cloud is the linear mean. A curve means $f(x)$ is still in the residual.

::: {.notes}
Left panel flat cloud is the linear mean assumption; right U-shape is missing curvature in $f(x)$. Pair with the smoothing section later. This is the first of four diagnostic figures—code was on the prior slide.
:::

## The residual QQ plot

![Two normal QQ plots of residuals. Left: points along the line. Right: heavy tails from a t distribution.](figures/generated/lm-qq.png){fig-alt="Left, Gaussian residuals follow the normal reference line. Right, residuals from a heavy-tailed draw flare at both ends." width="92%"}

Same reading as the [shape figures](#sec-qq-shapes). A line supports the Gaussian assumption behind the $t$ and $F$ tests. A flare is a heavy tail, and the next slide changes the model for $Y$.

::: {.notes}
Gaussian residuals on the line; $t$ residuals flare both tails. Same vocabulary as the opening QQ shapes. Flare here motivates changing the family for $Y$, not only the mean structure.
:::

## Scale against location {#sec-lm-scale-location}

![Two scale-location plots. Left: a flat smooth of the square-root absolute residual. Right: the smooth rises because the variance grows with x.](figures/generated/lm-scale-location.png){fig-alt="Left, the square root of the absolute residual stays level across fitted values. Right, it rises as the fitted value increases." width="96%"}

A flat smooth is [constant variance]{.mark}, the Gauss–Markov condition. A rise is a variance that travels with the mean: [generalised least squares](#sec-ols-replacements), or a family in which the variance depends on $\mu$.

::: {.notes}
Flat smooth of $\sqrt{|\text{residual}|}$ is constant variance; rising smooth is variance with mean. Link to $\phi V(\mu)$ in GLMs and to GLS on the replacements slide.
:::

## Leverage and Cook's distance

![Two residual-versus-leverage plots. Left: points near the origin, inside the Cook contours. Right: one point far to the right with a large residual.](figures/generated/lm-leverage.png){fig-alt="Left, residuals sit at small leverage. Right, one observation has high leverage and a large residual, beyond a Cook's-distance contour." width="96%"}

[Leverage]{.mark} $h_{ii}$ is the diagonal of the hat matrix. A common cut is $2p/n$ or $3p/n$ from Belsley, Kuh, and Welsch (1980). The contours are Cook's distance 0.5 and 1.

::: {.notes}
Leverage $h_{ii}$ from the hat matrix; cuts $2p/n$ or $3p/n$ from BKW. Cook contours 0.5 and 1 on the figure. High leverage plus large residual is the point to name on the right panel.

**Going further.** The leverage $h_{ii} = \mathbf{x}_i^{\top}(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{x}_i$ lies in $[0, 1]$ and the $h_{ii}$ sum to $p$, so their mean is $p/n$ and $2p/n$ flags twice the average. Cook's distance is $D_i = e_i^2 h_{ii} / \{p\, \hat{\sigma}^2 (1 - h_{ii})^2\}$, the scaled change in all fitted values when row $i$ is deleted; it combines a large residual with a large leverage. A cut of 1 corresponds roughly to moving $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ to the edge of a 50% confidence region (Cook and Weisberg, *Residuals and Influence in Regression*, 1982). For a GLM the same quantities come from the weighted hat matrix of the final IRLS step.
:::

## Cook's distance, row by row {#sec-lm-cooks}

![Two Cook's distance plots by observation number. Left: every bar is small. Right: one observation stands far above the others.](figures/generated/lm-cooks-distance.png){fig-alt="Left, Cook's distance for each of 80 rows stays below 0.1. Right, the last row, a high-leverage point with a large residual, has a Cook's distance far above 1 while the other rows stay near zero." width="96%"}

`which = 4`. Each bar is how far all the fitted values move when that row is deleted. A bar above 1 is a row to [inspect]{.mark}, not a row to delete.

::: {.notes}
Same fits as the leverage slide. The right panel has one point at $x = 4$ with a large residual: its bar dwarfs the rest. Ask what they would do with it: check the record, refit without it, and report both; do not drop it silently.

**Going further.** $D_i = \frac{\sum_j (\hat y_j - \hat y_{j(i)})^2}{p\,\hat\sigma^2}$, where $\hat y_{j(i)}$ is the fit without row $i$; the deletion formula gives it from one fit as $D_i = \frac{r_i^2}{p}\frac{h_{ii}}{1 - h_{ii}}$ with $r_i$ the standardised residual. The threshold 1 is a convention; $4/n$ is another, more sensitive one (Fox, *Applied Regression Analysis and Generalized Linear Models*).
:::

## Cook's distance against leverage {#sec-lm-cooks-leverage}

![Two plots of Cook's distance against leverage over one minus leverage, with dotted contours of equal standardised residual. Left: points near the origin. Right: one point far to the right and high.](figures/generated/lm-cooks-leverage.png){fig-alt="Left, all points sit at small leverage and small Cook's distance. Right, one point has the largest leverage ratio and a Cook's distance far above the rest, beyond the outer dotted contour." width="96%"}

`which = 6`. The horizontal axis is $h_{ii}/(1 - h_{ii})$, the dotted lines are equal standardised residuals. A point far right and high combines [leverage]{.mark} with a large residual.

::: {.notes}
This plot separates the two ingredients of Cook's distance: leverage on the horizontal axis, the residual through the contours. A high-leverage point on a contour near zero is influential in principle but agrees with the fit; one on an outer contour moves it.
:::

## ANOVA and ANCOVA {.center .pitfall-divider background-gradient="linear-gradient(160deg, #f7f4ef 0%, #f6e2c4 100%)"}

## A regression describes a conditional function {#sec-anova-conditional}

A regression model targets one function of $Y$ [given]{.mark} the covariates. For a Gaussian linear model it is the arithmetic mean; other models target other functions.

| Model | Conditional function of $Y$ |
| --- | --- |
| Linear regression | mean, $\mathbb{E}(Y \mid x) = \mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta$ |
| Logistic regression | probability, $\mathrm{logit}\,\Pr(Y = 1 \mid x) = \mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta$ |
| Quantile regression | quantile, $Q_\tau(Y \mid x) = \mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta$ |
| Cox regression | hazard, $\log \lambda(t \mid x) = \log\lambda_0(t) + \mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta$ |

An ANOVA compares that function between the groups formed by the levels of a factor. 📝 Olszewski, [*A brief story of ANOVA*](references/anova-interpreation.pdf) (2025).

::: {.notes}
His first three pages: the regression gives a conditional function; levels of a categorical predictor form groups; "conditional" means the function is computed within each group. The ANOVA question is the same whichever function the model targets, which is why the name survives in logistic and quantile regression.

**Going further.** The conditional mean minimises squared error, the conditional median absolute error, and the conditional $\tau$-quantile the check loss $\rho_\tau(u) = u\{\tau - \mathbf{1}(u < 0)\}$ (Koenker and Bassett, *Econometrica*, 1978). A factor with $L$ levels enters as $L - 1$ indicator columns, so the conditional function takes one value per group, and the main effect is the hypothesis that those $L$ values are equal.
:::

## One global question, or one comparison {.smaller #sec-anova-vs-contrast}

Body mass index with four levels: underweight, normal, overweight, obese. With two levels the question is a $t$ test; with four, two questions part ways.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**ANOVA: a main effect**

- Do the four levels [jointly]{.mark} move the mean?
- $H_0: \mu_{\text{under}} = \mu_{\text{normal}} = \mu_{\text{over}} = \mu_{\text{obese}}$
- 3 degrees of freedom, one $F$ or $\chi^2$
- It says whether the factor matters, not which levels differ
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Contrasts: simple effects**

- A [contrast]{.mark} is a function of the coefficients, $\mathbf{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta$
- obese against normal, or obese against the mean of the other three
- 1 degree of freedom each; several need [multiplicity control](#sec-multiplicity)
- Their coding in R is the [contrasts block](#sec-contr-treatment) of the design hour
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Olszewski's pages 3 to 6. A comparison between individual groups is a simple effect; the global question is the main effect. Planned contrasts answer the research question; Tukey's all-pairwise and Dunnett's all-against-baseline are families of simple effects. The ANOVA on a three-level factor is the joint test of two such contrasts, which the next slides compute.

**Going further.** With treatment coding the coefficients are differences from the reference, so $\mu_B - \mu_A = \beta_B$ and $\mu_C - \mu_B = \beta_C - \beta_B$: a contrast is a row vector applied to $\boldsymbol\beta$. Contrasts with $\sum_k c_k = 0$ on the group means are estimable whatever the coding, and their estimate and standard error do not depend on it.
:::

## The ANOVA splits the variability {#sec-anova-ss}

With $k$ groups, $n_j$ rows in group $j$, and $N$ rows in all:

$$
\underbrace{\sum_{j}\sum_{i} (Y_{ij} - \bar Y)^2}_{\text{total}} = \underbrace{\sum_{j} n_j(\bar Y_j - \bar Y)^2}_{\text{between groups}} + \underbrace{\sum_{j}\sum_{i} (Y_{ij} - \bar Y_j)^2}_{\text{within groups}}
$$

$$
F = \frac{\mathrm{SS}_{\text{between}}/(k - 1)}{\mathrm{SS}_{\text{within}}/(N - k)} \;\sim\; F_{k-1,\,N-k} \quad \text{under } H_0
$$

Each sum of squares is divided by its degrees of freedom: a [mean square]{.mark}. A large $F$ means the group means are far apart compared with the spread inside each group.

::: {.notes}
Write the identity from left to right: total spread around the grand mean equals spread of the group means plus spread around each group mean. The cross term vanishes because residuals sum to zero within each group. Then the ratio. The next slide lets the room move both ingredients.

**Going further.** The within mean square is the pooled variance estimate, unbiased for $\sigma^2$ whatever the means; the between mean square has expectation $\sigma^2 + \sum_j n_j(\mu_j - \bar\mu)^2/(k - 1)$, so the ratio is near 1 under $H_0$ and grows with the spacing. Cochran's theorem gives the two sums of squares independent $\chi^2$ distributions under Gaussian errors, hence the exact $F$.
:::

## Try it: what moves the $F$ ratio {.anova-ojs #sec-anova-explorer}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof anovaCtrl = Inputs.form({
  spacing: Inputs.range([0, 20], {value: 11, step: 1, label: "Mean spacing"}),
  spread: Inputs.range([2, 20], {value: 4.5, step: 0.5, label: "Within spread"})
})
viewof anovaDraw = Inputs.button("Generate data")
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
anovaChart = {
  const labels = ["A", "B", "C"], colours = ["#1d4e89", "#c45c26", "#0e4d3a"];
  const n = 8, W = 920, H = 330, left = 50, plotW = 520, top = 18, bottom = 300;
  const rng = d3.randomNormal.source(d3.randomLcg(20261005 + anovaDraw))(0, 1);
  const data = [];
  labels.forEach((g, j) => {
    const z = Array.from({length: n}, rng);
    const m = d3.mean(z), s = d3.deviation(z);
    z.forEach((v, i) => data.push({
      j, i, y: Math.max(0, Math.min(100, 50 + (j - 1) * anovaCtrl.spacing + anovaCtrl.spread * (v - m) / s))
    }));
  });
  const y = d3.scaleLinear().domain([0, 100]).range([bottom, top]);
  const xc = j => left + 90 + j * 170;
  const svg = d3.create("svg").attr("viewBox", [0, 0, W, H]).attr("width", W).style("font", "15px sans-serif");
  svg.append("g").attr("transform", `translate(${left},0)`).call(d3.axisLeft(y).ticks(5));
  const grand = svg.append("line").attr("x1", left).attr("x2", left + plotW)
    .attr("stroke", "#1c2b24").attr("stroke-dasharray", "5 4");
  const grandLab = svg.append("text").attr("x", left + plotW).attr("text-anchor", "end").attr("fill", "#1c2b24");
  const meanLines = labels.map((g, j) => svg.append("line").attr("x1", xc(j) - 48).attr("x2", xc(j) + 48)
    .attr("stroke", colours[j]).attr("stroke-width", 3));
  const meanLabs = labels.map((g, j) => svg.append("text").attr("x", xc(j)).attr("y", top + 4)
    .attr("text-anchor", "middle").attr("fill", colours[j]));
  const panel = svg.append("g").attr("transform", `translate(${left + plotW + 40},${top + 20})`);
  const line = (k, label) => {
    panel.append("text").attr("y", k * 44).attr("fill", "#5c6b63").text(label);
    return panel.append("text").attr("y", k * 44 + 22).attr("font-size", 20).attr("fill", "#1c2b24");
  };
  const tWithin = line(0, "Within variation"), tBetween = line(1, "Between variation"),
        tF = line(2, "ANOVA, α = 0.05"), tP = line(3, "");
  const verdict = panel.append("text").attr("y", 4 * 44 + 30).attr("font-size", 22).attr("font-weight", "bold");
  function update() {
    const groups = labels.map((g, j) => data.filter(d => d.j === j).map(d => d.y));
    const N = data.length, k = groups.length, gm = d3.mean(data, d => d.y);
    const means = groups.map(v => d3.mean(v));
    const ssb = d3.sum(groups, (v, j) => v.length * (means[j] - gm) ** 2);
    const ssw = d3.sum(groups, (v, j) => d3.sum(v, x => (x - means[j]) ** 2));
    const msb = ssb / (k - 1), msw = ssw / (N - k), F = msb / msw, p = fPvalue(F, k - 1, N - k);
    grand.attr("y1", y(gm)).attr("y2", y(gm));
    grandLab.attr("y", y(gm) - 6).text(`grand mean ${gm.toFixed(0)}`);
    meanLines.forEach((l, j) => l.attr("y1", y(means[j])).attr("y2", y(means[j])));
    meanLabs.forEach((t, j) => t.text(`Group ${labels[j]} · mean ${means[j].toFixed(0)}`));
    tWithin.text(`mean square ${msw.toFixed(1)}`);
    tBetween.text(`mean square ${msb.toFixed(1)}`);
    tF.text(`F = ${F.toFixed(2)} on ${k - 1} and ${N - k} df`);
    tP.text(p < 0.001 ? "p < 0.001" : `p = ${p.toFixed(3)}`);
    verdict.text(p < 0.05 ? "Evidence of a difference" : "No clear evidence")
      .attr("fill", p < 0.05 ? "#1d4e89" : "#c45c26");
  }
  svg.selectAll("circle").data(data).join("circle")
    .attr("cx", d => xc(d.j) + (d.i - (n - 1) / 2) * 10)
    .attr("cy", d => y(d.y)).attr("r", 6)
    .attr("fill", d => colours[d.j]).attr("fill-opacity", 0.75).style("cursor", "ns-resize")
    .call(d3.drag().on("drag", function (event, d) {
      d.y = Math.max(0, Math.min(100, y.invert(event.y)));
      d3.select(this).attr("cy", y(d.y));
      update();
    }));
  update();
  return svg.node();
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| output: false
function lgammaFn(x) {
  const c = [0.99999999999980993, 676.5203681218851, -1259.1392167224028, 771.32342877765313,
    -176.61502916214059, 12.507343278686905, -0.13857109526572012, 9.9843695780195716e-6, 1.5056327351493116e-7];
  if (x < 0.5) return Math.log(Math.PI / Math.sin(Math.PI * x)) - lgammaFn(1 - x);
  x -= 1;
  let a = c[0];
  const t = x + 7.5;
  for (let i = 1; i < 9; i++) a += c[i] / (x + i);
  return 0.5 * Math.log(2 * Math.PI) + (x + 0.5) * Math.log(t) - t + Math.log(a);
}
function betaCf(a, b, x) {
  const tiny = 1e-300;
  let c = 1, d = 1 - (a + b) * x / (a + 1);
  if (Math.abs(d) < tiny) d = tiny;
  d = 1 / d;
  let h = d;
  for (let m = 1; m <= 300; m++) {
    const m2 = 2 * m;
    let aa = m * (b - m) * x / ((a - 1 + m2) * (a + m2));
    d = 1 + aa * d; if (Math.abs(d) < tiny) d = tiny;
    c = 1 + aa / c; if (Math.abs(c) < tiny) c = tiny;
    d = 1 / d; h *= d * c;
    aa = -(a + m) * (a + b + m) * x / ((a + m2) * (a + 1 + m2));
    d = 1 + aa * d; if (Math.abs(d) < tiny) d = tiny;
    c = 1 + aa / c; if (Math.abs(c) < tiny) c = tiny;
    d = 1 / d;
    const del = d * c; h *= del;
    if (Math.abs(del - 1) < 3e-14) break;
  }
  return h;
}
function incBeta(x, a, b) {
  if (x <= 0) return 0;
  if (x >= 1) return 1;
  const bt = Math.exp(lgammaFn(a + b) - lgammaFn(a) - lgammaFn(b) + a * Math.log(x) + b * Math.log(1 - x));
  return x < (a + 1) / (a + b + 2) ? bt * betaCf(a, b, x) / a : 1 - bt * betaCf(b, a, 1 - x) / b;
}
function fPvalue(F, d1, d2) {
  if (!(F > 0) || !isFinite(F)) return F === Infinity ? 0 : 1;
  return incBeta(d2 / (d2 + d1 * F), d2 / 2, d1 / 2);
}
```

::: {.notes}
Three groups of eight, simulated in the browser. Move the mean spacing to zero: $F$ falls near 1 and the verdict turns. Widen the spread: the same spacing stops being evidence. Drag one dot far up: one observation moves its group mean and inflates the within mean square at the same time. "Generate data" draws a new sample with the same spacing and spread. The $p$-value comes from the $F$ distribution on 2 and 21 degrees of freedom, computed in the page.

The layout reproduces an interactive one-way ANOVA view that a chat assistant drew as a built-in component; this version is written for the deck in Observable JavaScript, with d3.
:::

## The $F$ distribution needs three conditions {#sec-anova-assumptions}

$F$ follows $F_{k-1,\,N-k}$ exactly when the residuals of the model underneath are:

::: {.incremental}
- [independent]{.mark}: one row does not inform another
- [Gaussian]{.mark}: normal within each group
- of [equal variance]{.mark}: the same spread in every group
:::

All three come from the least-squares fit, not from the ANOVA. Balance is not required, but it makes the $F$ test far less sensitive to unequal variances.

::: {.notes}
Olszewski's page 12: every ANOVA assumption is an assumption of the OLS estimation underneath, read per group. The order matters: independence is the one that cannot be repaired by a large sample.

**Going further.** With equal group sizes the $F$ test keeps close to its nominal level under moderate non-normality and under variance ratios up to about 4; with unequal sizes, a large variance in the smallest group makes it liberal and in the largest group conservative (Box, *Annals of Mathematical Statistics*, 1954). Welch's heteroscedastic $F$, or the GLS fit on the "assumption fails" slide, removes the equal-variance condition. Dependence among rows inflates the type I error whatever the balance, which is the pseudoreplication problem of the design hour.
:::

## ANOVA is a joint test on a model {#sec-anova-joint}

- It is not a test: it uses an $F$ or a $\chi^2$ statistic
- It is not a model: it runs on a fitted model
- It asks whether the levels of a factor [jointly]{.mark} move the mean: all the contrasts of that factor at once, not one pair

`anova(lm(y ~ group), lm(y ~ 1))` and `summary(aov(lm(y ~ group)))` give the same $F$. 📝 Olszewski, [*A brief story of ANOVA*](references/anova-interpreation.pdf) (2025).

::: {.notes}
Read the three bullets as his three questions: test, model, then what. In his example a three-level factor gives $F = 174.6$ on 2 and 87 degrees of freedom whether you call `aov`, compare two nested models with `anova`, or test the two contrasts $\mu_{A1} - \mu_{A2}$ and $(\mu_{A1} + \mu_{A2})/2 - \mu_{A3}$ jointly with `emmeans`. The "variance" in analysis of variance is the residual variance that drops when the factor enters.

**Going further.** For a factor with $L$ levels the ANOVA null is $\mathbf{C}\boldsymbol\beta = \mathbf{0}$ for any full-rank $(L-1)$-row contrast matrix $\mathbf{C}$; the Wald statistic $(\mathbf{C}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})^{\top}\{\mathbf{C}\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})\mathbf{C}^{\top}\}^{-1}(\mathbf{C}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})/(L-1)$ does not depend on which $\mathbf{C}$ is chosen. In the Gaussian linear model Wald, score, and likelihood-ratio tests coincide and give the exact $F$; in a GLM they agree only asymptotically, and the same partition is the analysis of deviance. The construction applies to any model that returns $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ and its covariance, including quantile, robust, and mixed models, which is what `emmeans::joint_tests()` exploits.
:::

## ANCOVA · a factor shifts the intercept {#sec-lm-ancova}

The height example is `Height ~ Age + Gender`. Gender is a factor, so R codes it as an indicator against a reference level. Women are the baseline in the printout. The line for women is $124.52 + 2.72\,\mathrm{Age}$. The line for men has the same slope and a higher intercept, $127.3 + 2.72\,\mathrm{Age}$.

That is an [analysis of covariance]{.mark}: one continuous covariate, one categorical factor, and a common slope unless you add `Age:Gender`. The gender coefficient is a difference of intercepts, not the raw difference of the two mean heights. The sums of squares for that fit still depend on [which ANOVA type](#sec-deviance) you ask for.

::: {.notes}
`Height~Age+Gender`: women $124.52+2.72\,\mathrm{Age}$, men same slope, higher intercept $127.3$. Gender coefficient is intercept difference, not raw mean difference. ANOVA type still matters for SS.
:::

## From the variance to the deviance: three tests {#sec-wald-rao-lrt}

Any model that returns estimates $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ and their [variance–covariance matrix]{.mark} $\widehat{\mathbf{V}} = \widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})$, variances on the diagonal and covariances off it, can test a main effect $H_0: \mathbf{C}\boldsymbol\beta = \mathbf{0}$, with $q$ rows in $\mathbf{C}$:

$$
W = (\mathbf{C}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})^{\top}\left(\mathbf{C}\widehat{\mathbf{V}}\mathbf{C}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\mathbf{C}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} \;\approx\; \chi^2_q \quad \text{under } H_0.
$$

That is the [Wald]{.mark} test. A model fitted by likelihood also has the Rao score test and the likelihood-ratio test. Term by term, the likelihood-ratio version is the [analysis of deviance]{.mark}; in the Gaussian linear model all three reduce to the ANOVA $F$.

::: {.notes}
Olszewski's pages 8 to 11. The variance–covariance matrix is the piece people forget: without it there is no joint test, only separate $t$ tests on each coefficient, which ignore their correlation. The ANOVA on a three-level factor is $W$ with $\mathbf{C}$ the two contrasts of the earlier slide, divided by $q = 2$.

**Going further.** With $\tilde{\boldsymbol\beta}$ the fit under $H_0$, the score test is $S = U(\tilde{\boldsymbol\beta})^{\top}\mathcal{I}(\tilde{\boldsymbol\beta})^{-1}U(\tilde{\boldsymbol\beta})$, with $U$ the gradient of the log-likelihood and $\mathcal{I}$ the Fisher information, and the likelihood-ratio test is $\mathrm{LR} = 2\{\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}) - \ell(\tilde{\boldsymbol\beta})\}$. Under regularity conditions all three are asymptotically $\chi^2_q$ and differ by $o_p(1)$ under the null and local alternatives (Rao, 1948; Wald, 1943; Wilks, 1938). In the Gaussian linear model with $\sigma^2$ estimated by maximum likelihood they satisfy $W \geq \mathrm{LR} \geq S$ (Berndt and Savin, *Econometrica*, 1977), and with the unbiased variance estimate each is a monotone function of the same $F$.
:::

## Wald, score, likelihood ratio, side by side {.smaller #sec-test-trinity}

| | Wald | Rao score | Likelihood ratio |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Model fitted | The full model only | The null model only | Both, nested |
| Statistic | $(\mathbf{C}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})^{\top}(\mathbf{C}\widehat{\mathbf{V}}\mathbf{C}^{\top})^{-1}\mathbf{C}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ | $U(\tilde{\boldsymbol\beta})^{\top}\mathcal{I}(\tilde{\boldsymbol\beta})^{-1}U(\tilde{\boldsymbol\beta})$ | $2\{\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}) - \ell(\tilde{\boldsymbol\beta})\}$ |
| Needs | $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ and $\widehat{\mathbf{V}}$: any model, including GEE, quantile, robust | A likelihood | A likelihood |
| Strengths | One fit; any contrast; a robust (sandwich) $\widehat{\mathbf{V}}$ | No fit under the alternative | Same answer on any scale of $\boldsymbol\beta$; usually the most accurate in small samples |
| Weaknesses | Changes with the scale of $\boldsymbol\beta$; breaks down under separation | Fewer implementations | Two fits; no likelihood, no test |

All three are asymptotically $\chi^2_q$ and agree for large samples. In the Gaussian linear model they give the same $F$.

::: {.notes}
Read the first row: which model has to be fitted. That decides what is practical. Wald needs only the full model, which is why `emmeans::joint_tests()` can run on almost anything. The score test needs only the null model; it is the classical Pearson $\chi^2$ for a contingency table. The likelihood ratio needs both.

**Going further.** The Wald statistic is not invariant to reparametrisation: testing $\beta = 0$ and $e^{\beta} = 1$ gives different $W$, while LR is unchanged. In logistic regression the Wald statistic can decrease as the effect grows, because the standard error grows faster (Hauck and Donner, *Journal of the American Statistical Association*, 1977); under complete separation $\hat\beta$ diverges and the Wald test has no power, while the likelihood ratio still works. Profile-likelihood intervals are the interval counterpart of the LR test.
:::

## Deviance is the residual sum of squares {#sec-glm-deviance}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
Lack of fit is measured by the [deviance]{.mark}. The null deviance $D_0$ compares the intercept-only model with the [saturated model]{.mark}. The residual deviance $D$ compares the fitted model with the saturated model. Maximising the log-likelihood is the same operation as making $D$ small.
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
![](figures/generated/sketch-nongauss-b-deviance.png){.sketch fig-alt="Hand-drawn log-likelihood axis with three dots, null in grey, fitted in blue, saturated in green; a long arrow D0 spans null to saturated and a shorter blue arrow D spans fitted to saturated, under the formula D equals 2 times l-sat minus l."}
:::
::::

For nested models the [likelihood-ratio statistic]{.mark} is the drop in deviance,

$$
D_{\text{small}} - D_{\text{large}} \sim \chi^2,
$$

with degrees of freedom equal to the number of extra parameters. In R that is `anova(model1, model2, test = "Chisq")`. This is the GLM form of the [analysis of deviance](#sec-wald-rao-lrt). The next four slides build it step by step: [the saturated model](#sec-saturated), [the likelihood ratio](#sec-glrt), [a worked table](#sec-deviance-toxo), and [the $F$ version](#sec-deviance-f).

::: {.notes}
Their pseudo-$R^2$ is $1 - D/D_0$. They say that several pseudo-$R^2$ exist, and that a nested comparison should be the likelihood-ratio test. AIC is the comparison they allow when the models are not nested: deviance, plus a penalty for the number of parameters.

**Going further.** The scaled deviance is $D/\phi = 2\{\ell_{\text{sat}} - \ell(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})\}$, and $\phi = 1$ for the Poisson and the Bernoulli. Wilks' theorem makes $(D_{\text{small}} - D_{\text{large}})/\phi$ approximately $\chi^2_q$ for nested models, with $p$ fixed and $n \to \infty$; when $\phi$ is estimated, as in the quasi-Poisson, the reference is an $F$ distribution (`test = "F"`). The residual deviance itself is $\chi^2_{n-p}$ only under small-dispersion asymptotics, large Poisson means or large binomial totals, because the saturated model gains a parameter with every observation. For 0/1 data the deviance is a function of the $\hat\pi_i$ alone and says nothing about fit; use a grouped check such as Hosmer–Lemeshow, or the residual plots. McCullagh and Nelder's *Generalized Linear Models* treats these limits.
:::

## The saturated model is the ceiling {#sec-saturated}

The [saturated model]{.mark} gives each row its own parameter, so its fitted mean is the observation itself, $\tilde\mu_i = Y_i$. No model with the same family has a higher log-likelihood, $\ell_{\text{sat}}$. It is a yardstick, not a candidate: it explains nothing. With $\theta$ the canonical parameter of the family, the deviance of a fit is its distance below that ceiling:

$$
D = 2\phi\{\ell_{\text{sat}} - \ell(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})\}
  = 2\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl[Y_i(\tilde\theta_i - \hat\theta_i) - b(\tilde\theta_i) + b(\hat\theta_i)\bigr].
$$ {#eq-deviance}

- Gaussian: $D = \sum_i (Y_i - \hat\mu_i)^2$, the residual sum of squares
- Poisson: $D = 2\sum_i \{Y_i \log(Y_i/\hat\mu_i) - (Y_i - \hat\mu_i)\}$, with $0 \log 0 = 0$
- Binomial, $Y_i$ positives out of $m_i$: $D = 2\sum_i \{Y_i \log(Y_i/\hat\mu_i) + (m_i - Y_i)\log\frac{m_i - Y_i}{m_i - \hat\mu_i}\}$

::: {.notes}
Say "one parameter per row" and let the room see why it cannot be the answer: it reproduces the data and predicts nothing. The deviance is the GLM's residual sum of squares, and the first bullet shows that literally. The source for this block is Brooms's lecture chapter, [*Analysis of deviance*](references/analysis_of_deviance.pdf) (2005), section 7.2.

**Going further.** In the exponential dispersion family $\ell = \sum_i \{Y_i\theta_i - b(\theta_i)\}/a_i(\phi) + c(Y_i, \phi)$, and the saturated fit sets $b'(\tilde\theta_i) = Y_i$. The $c(Y_i, \phi)$ terms are the same in both fits and cancel, which is why the deviance does not depend on them. Each row contributes a non-negative term, $d_i$, and the deviance residual is $\mathrm{sign}(Y_i - \hat\mu_i)\sqrt{d_i}$. When the rows are grouped, the saturated model depends on the grouping: the deviance of 34 city totals is not the deviance of the same data written as 697 individual 0/1 rows, although differences between nested models are the same.
:::

## Two nested fits, one likelihood ratio {#sec-glrt}

A reduced model with $q$ parameters sits inside a full model with $p$. The [generalised likelihood ratio]{.mark} compares their maximised likelihoods:

$$
\Lambda = \frac{\hat L_R}{\hat L_F} \in (0, 1],
\qquad
-2\log\Lambda
  = \frac{D_R - D_F}{\phi}
  \;\approx\; \chi^2_{p-q}
  \quad\text{under } H_0: \beta_{q+1} = \cdots = \beta_p = 0.
$$ {#eq-glrt}

$\Lambda$ near 1 says the extra terms add little. Write each likelihood relative to the saturated one and $\ell_{\text{sat}}$ cancels: the test is a drop in deviance. The same ratio against the saturated model is a goodness-of-fit test, $D_F/\phi \approx \chi^2_{n-p}$, but that approximation is often poor.

::: {.notes}
Read @eq-glrt from left to right: a ratio of likelihoods, its log, and the deviance difference. The saturated model is the common reference that cancels. Then the warning in the last sentence: the difference between two models is trustworthy, the absolute deviance of one model much less so.

**Going further.** Wilks' theorem gives the $\chi^2_{p-q}$ limit with $p$ fixed and $n \to \infty$. The goodness-of-fit version is a different limit: the saturated model gains a parameter with every row, so $D_F/\phi \approx \chi^2_{n-p}$ holds only under small-dispersion asymptotics, large Poisson means or large binomial totals in each row (McCullagh and Nelder, *Generalized Linear Models*, 1989, section 4.4). For 0/1 data the residual deviance depends on the fitted values alone and carries no information about fit.
:::

## Toxoplasmosis: a cubic on rainfall {#sec-deviance-toxo}

![Proportion testing positive for toxoplasmosis in 34 cities against annual rainfall, point size proportional to the number tested, with the intercept-only fit as a dashed line and the cubic logistic fit as an orange curve.](figures/generated/toxo-deviance.png){fig-alt="Scatter of 34 city proportions between 0 and 1 against rainfall from 1600 to 2300 mm. A dashed horizontal line sits near 0.51. An orange curve rises to about 0.56 near 1800 mm, falls to about 0.42 near 2100 mm, then rises to about 0.6." width="80%"}

Efron's 34 cities. The deviance falls from 74.21 on 33 df (intercept only) to 62.63 on 30 df (cubic in rainfall): a drop of 11.58 on 3 df, so $\chi^2_3$ gives $p = 0.009$. But 62.63 on 30 df is itself about twice its degrees of freedom.

::: {.notes}
Worked example from Brooms's section 7.3 and the S-PLUS output in [the chapter](references/analysis_of_deviance.pdf), refitted in R by `scripts/generate-slide-figures.R`; the numbers are in `figures/generated/estimates.json`. Published data (Efron, 1986, *Journal of the American Statistical Association*), not a simulation and not CA-SYS or SPRUCE. The sequential table in the chapter adds one power at a time: the linear term drops the deviance by 0.12, the quadratic by 0.00, the cubic by 11.45, the quartic by 0.19, the quintic by 1.25. Only the cubic moves it.

Ask the room what a residual deviance twice its degrees of freedom means for a binomial, where $\phi$ is fixed at 1. The next slide answers.

**Going further.** A sequential (Type I) table depends on the order of the terms; here the order is the natural one, increasing powers, so it answers "does the next power help, given the lower ones?". Centring rainfall reduces the collinearity between powers but does not remove it: the chapter's correlation matrix shows $-0.95$ between the quadratic and quartic coefficients. A spline or a fractional polynomial, from the smoothing section, is the modern alternative to choosing a polynomial degree by sequential tests.
:::

## An estimated dispersion turns the $\chi^2$ into an $F$ {#sec-deviance-f}

When $\phi$ is not known, estimate it from the full model, $\tilde\phi = D_F/(n-p)$, and divide:

$$
F = \frac{(D_R - D_F)/(p-q)}{D_F/(n-p)} \;\approx\; F_{p-q,\,n-p}.
$$ {#eq-deviance-f}

For the Gaussian linear model $D$ is the residual sum of squares and @eq-deviance-f is the [ANOVA $F$]{.mark}, exactly: the analysis of deviance contains the analysis of variance. For the toxoplasmosis cubic, $\hat\phi \approx 2$, and the quasi-binomial $F$ is 1.99 on 3 and 30 df, $p = 0.14$. The cubic that looked convincing under $\phi = 1$ is within the extra-binomial noise.

::: {.notes}
Brooms's section 7.4 shows the exact case: with Normal errors and the identity link, $(D_R - D_F)/\phi$ is the extra regression sum of squares over $\sigma^2$, independent of $D_F/\phi = \mathrm{SSR}/\sigma^2$, so the ratio is exactly $F$. Elsewhere it is an approximation. The two estimates of $\phi$ for the cubic are 2.09 from the deviance and 1.94 from the Pearson statistic; R's `quasibinomial` uses Pearson, which gives the 1.99. Both say the same thing: the cities vary more than a binomial allows, and the $p$-value moves from 0.009 to 0.14.

**Going further.** The Pearson estimate $\hat\phi = \sum_i (Y_i - \hat\mu_i)^2/\{V(\hat\mu_i)(n-p)\}$ is consistent under the mean–variance model alone; the deviance estimate is biased when counts are small. Overdispersion here has two usual readings: unmeasured city-level variation, which a beta-binomial or a city random effect would model, or a mean function that is still wrong. The quasi-likelihood $F$ treats it as a variance inflation only. In R: `anova(fit0, fit, test = "F")` on a `quasibinomial` or `quasipoisson` fit.
:::

## The $F$ of the linearised fit {#sec-irls-f}

A GLM is fitted as a weighted linear model on the link scale. At convergence, with the [working response]{.mark}

$$
z_i = \hat\eta_i + (Y_i - \hat\mu_i)\,g'(\hat\mu_i),
\qquad
w_i = \frac{1}{V(\hat\mu_i)\,g'(\hat\mu_i)^2},
\qquad
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{z}.
$$ {#eq-irls}

$z_i$ is a first-order expansion of $g$ around $\hat\mu_i$, not $g(Y_i)$, so a zero count is no problem. Its weighted residual sum of squares is the [Pearson statistic]{.mark}, $\sum_i w_i(z_i - \hat\eta_i)^2 = \sum_i (Y_i - \hat\mu_i)^2/V(\hat\mu_i)$. An $F$ test on this weighted fit, with the weights held at the full model, is therefore the Wald $F$, $W/(q\hat\phi)$. With a Gaussian family and the identity link, $z_i = Y_i$, $w_i = 1$, and it is the ordinary ANOVA.

::: {.notes}
This slide answers "can I just run an $F$ test after the link?". Yes, in this precise sense: the link is applied to the mean through the linearisation, the weights carry the variance function, and the residual mean square is the Pearson $\hat\phi$. It is not the same as transforming $Y$ and running `lm`: that would put $g(Y_i)$ on the left, which is the transformation the [link stays on the mean](#sec-glm-versus-transform) slide rejects.

**Going further.** Iteratively reweighted least squares is Fisher scoring: each step regresses $\mathbf{z}$ on $\mathbf{X}$ with weights $\mathbf{W}$ evaluated at the current $\hat{\boldsymbol\mu}$, and the fixed point is the maximum-likelihood estimate (Nelder and Wedderburn, 1972). Holding $\mathbf{W}$ fixed, the extra weighted sum of squares for $H_0: \mathbf{C}\boldsymbol\beta = \mathbf{0}$ is $(\mathbf{C}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})^{\top}\{\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{C}^{\top}\}^{-1}\mathbf{C}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$, which is $\hat\phi$ times the Wald statistic of the [three-tests slide](#sec-wald-rao-lrt). It agrees with the deviance $F$ of @eq-deviance-f to first order, and differs from it when the effect is large or the sample small; the likelihood-ratio version is usually the more accurate.
:::

## The three tests in R {#sec-anova-r}

::: {.codewindow .r}
main-effects.R
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
fit  <- lm(y ~ bmi + age, data = d)
fit0 <- update(fit, . ~ . - bmi)
anova(fit0, fit)                         # F: the Gaussian linear model
car::Anova(fit, type = 2)                # Type II, each term after the others
emmeans::joint_tests(fit)                # Wald, on any model emmeans supports

gfit  <- glm(count ~ bmi + age, family = poisson, data = d)
gfit0 <- update(gfit, . ~ . - bmi)
anova(gfit0, gfit, test = "LRT")         # likelihood ratio: drop in deviance
anova(gfit0, gfit, test = "Rao")         # score test
car::Anova(gfit, type = 2, test.statistic = "Wald")
```
:::

`fit0` is the model without the factor. A nested comparison is the [likelihood-ratio]{.mark} route; `joint_tests()` is the Wald route, and it accepts GLS, GEE, mixed, and quantile fits.

::: {.notes}
Point at the pairs: `anova(fit0, fit)` compares two models, `car::Anova()` and `joint_tests()` test terms inside one model. `test = "LRT"` and `test = "Chisq"` are the same. For a quasi-Poisson or a negative-binomial fit with estimated dispersion, use `test = "F"`.
:::

## Which R function gives which type {.smaller #sec-anova-functions}

| Function | Type | Models | Watch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `aov()` | I | Linear model | ⚠️ The order of the terms changes the result |
| `anova()` | I or III | Most models, including GLMs | Usually a comparison of two models |
| `car::Anova()` | II or III | Most models | Type III needs `contr.sum` |
| `emmeans::joint_tests()` | III | GLS, GEE, mixed, quantile, robust | Tests [estimated marginal means]{.mark}, not raw means |

Choose the type for the question, then the function that gives it.

::: {.notes}
The table is Olszewski's last-but-one page, shortened. Type II is the safe default for main effects without an interaction; `joint_tests()` is the route when the model is not a plain `lm`, and it does not need the contrasts to be set by hand.

**Going further.** `emmeans` builds a reference grid with every combination of factor levels, predicts at each, and averages those predictions with equal weights by default; in an unbalanced design that grid is not the observed covariate distribution, so the "marginal mean" is a standardised mean, not the sample mean. The denominator degrees of freedom for mixed models can use the Satterthwaite or Kenward–Roger approximations, and a sandwich covariance can be passed in for heteroscedastic data (Lenth, *emmeans* vignettes).
:::

## Favour the model-based test, and generalise the model {.smaller #sec-anova-fails}

| Assumption violated | Use instead | Comment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Equal variance | GLS with the same terms, `nlme::gls(y ~ group, weights = varIdent(form = ~ 1 | group))`; start there, without a Levene pretest | The covariance structure has to be specified: start unstructured, simplify if it does not fit |
| Independence (repeated, clustered) | GLS with a correlation, GEE, or a linear mixed model | GEE: asymptotic inference only. Mixed model: choose the random effects |
| Gaussian residuals | GEE, or a permutation ANOVA | GEE: asymptotic only. Permutation: heavy computation |
| Outliers | A robust linear (mixed) model | Heavy computation |

Each keeps the [arithmetic mean]{.mark} in $H_0$, and `emmeans::joint_tests()` gives the Wald test on any of them. A switch to Kruskal–Wallis does not: it tests stochastic superiority.

::: {.notes}
Olszewski's page 14, nearly verbatim in structure. His example, seed 100: three groups with standard deviations 1, 2, and 5. The ordinary ANOVA gives $p = 0.142$; the GLS fit with a variance per group gives $p = 0.011$ for the same means. No Levene pretest is needed: start from the GLS fit.

**Going further.** With $\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon_{ij}) = \sigma_j^2$, GLS weights each group by $1/\hat\sigma_j^2$, which is the multi-group generalisation of the Welch test; the denominator degrees of freedom shrink because the variances are estimated, which is why `joint_tests(..., mode = "df.error")` reports 85 rather than 87. Permutation ANOVA is exact only under exchangeability, so with unequal variances it should permute a studentised statistic (the Welch-type $F$), for the same reason as the two-group case.
:::

## ⚠️ Do not reach for `aov()` {.fit-fig #sec-anova-type}

::: {.callout-warning title="`aov()` is Type I: the order of the terms changes the answer"}
In the sketch the treatment $F$ is 16.6 or 38.7, depending only on the order of entry. Use `car::Anova()` or `emmeans::joint_tests()`, and name the type in the methods.
:::

![A warning that aov() in R is Type I ANOVA, so the test of treatment depends on whether baseline or treatment is entered first.](figures/sources/ancova-type-i-order.jpeg){fig-alt="Four rows. lm, car::Anova with type 2, and permuco are marked safe. aov is marked not safe, because the order of baseline and treatment changes the sums of squares." width="60%"}

::: {.notes}
Olszewski's last page: the method is balanced, 30 per group, no missing data; a baseline correlated $r = 0.35$ with the outcome is enough. `summary(aov(PD ~ Method + PD_Bas))` gives $F = 3.43$ for Method, $p = 0.069$; with the baseline first, $F = 13.59$, $p = 0.0005$. Type II gives 13.59 in both orders. The image is his LinkedIn sketch of the same point ([post](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:7444337265641684992/)).
:::

## Type I, II, and III answer different questions {.smaller #sec-deviance}

For two factors $A$ and $B$, the sum of squares charged to each term ([Type I, II, III SS explained](https://www.r-bloggers.com/2011/03/anova-%E2%80%93-type-iiiiii-ss-explained/)):

| Type | $A$ | $B$ | $A \times B$ | Use when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| I, sequential | $\mathrm{SS}(A)$ | $\mathrm{SS}(B \mid A)$ | $\mathrm{SS}(AB \mid A, B)$ | the order of entry is the scientific order |
| II, hierarchical | $\mathrm{SS}(A \mid B)$ | $\mathrm{SS}(B \mid A)$ | $\mathrm{SS}(AB \mid A, B)$ | no interaction; then it is the most powerful |
| III, marginal | $\mathrm{SS}(A \mid B, AB)$ | $\mathrm{SS}(B \mid A, AB)$ | $\mathrm{SS}(AB \mid A, B)$ | an interaction is present; needs `contr.sum` |

With balanced data the three coincide. They part ways as soon as the cell sizes differ, because $A$ and $B$ are then correlated.

::: {.notes}
The three differences to keep: Type I depends on the order; Type II tests each main effect after the other but assumes no interaction; Type III tests each main effect in the presence of the interaction, which is only interpretable with sum-to-zero contrasts and a meaningful "average" main effect. If the interaction is clearly present, the main effects themselves are rarely the question: report the simple effects.

**Going further.** Type II respects marginality (Nelder, *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series A*, 1977): a main effect is not tested in the presence of an interaction that contains it. Type III does test it, and its sums of squares depend on the contrast coding, so it is meaningful only with sum-to-zero contrasts (`contr.sum`), not R's default treatment contrasts. For a GLM the same choice applies to the deviance partition.
:::

## Try it: Type I, II, and III on an unbalanced design {.anova-ojs #sec-anova-types-explorer}

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof typesCtrl = Inputs.form({
  a: Inputs.range([0, 3], {value: 1, step: 0.25, label: "Effect of A"}),
  b: Inputs.range([0, 3], {value: 1, step: 0.25, label: "Effect of B"}),
  ab: Inputs.range([-3, 3], {value: 0, step: 0.25, label: "Interaction A × B"}),
  u: Inputs.range([0, 8], {value: 6, step: 1, label: "Imbalance"})
})
viewof typesDraw = Inputs.button("Generate data")
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
typesView = {
  const rng = d3.randomNormal.source(d3.randomLcg(20261005 + typesDraw))(0, 1);
  const base = 10, u = typesCtrl.u, rows = [];
  for (const a of [-1, 1]) for (const b of [-1, 1]) {
    const nCell = a * b > 0 ? base + u : base - u;
    for (let r = 0; r < nCell; r++) rows.push({a, b,
      y: 10 + typesCtrl.a / 2 * a + typesCtrl.b / 2 * b + typesCtrl.ab / 2 * a * b + rng()});
  }
  const cols = {one: d => 1, a: d => d.a, b: d => d.b, ab: d => d.a * d.b};
  function rss(names) {
    const X = rows.map(d => names.map(nm => cols[nm](d))), p = names.length;
    const XtX = Array.from({length: p}, (_, r) => Array.from({length: p}, (_, c) => d3.sum(X, x => x[r] * x[c])));
    const Xty = Array.from({length: p}, (_, r) => d3.sum(X, (x, i) => x[r] * rows[i].y));
    const M = XtX.map((row, r) => [...row, Xty[r]]);
    for (let c = 0; c < p; c++) {
      let piv = c;
      for (let r = c + 1; r < p; r++) if (Math.abs(M[r][c]) > Math.abs(M[piv][c])) piv = r;
      [M[c], M[piv]] = [M[piv], M[c]];
      for (let r = 0; r < p; r++) if (r !== c) {
        const f = M[r][c] / M[c][c];
        for (let k = c; k <= p; k++) M[r][k] -= f * M[c][k];
      }
    }
    const beta = M.map((row, r) => row[p] / row[r]);
    return d3.sum(X, (x, i) => (rows[i].y - d3.sum(x, (v, k) => v * beta[k])) ** 2);
  }
  const R = {
    one: rss(["one"]), a: rss(["one", "a"]), b: rss(["one", "b"]), ab: rss(["one", "a", "b"]),
    full: rss(["one", "a", "b", "ab"]), noA: rss(["one", "b", "ab"]), noB: rss(["one", "a", "ab"])
  };
  const N = rows.length, dfe = N - 4, mse = R.full / dfe;
  const ssAB = R.ab - R.full;
  const table = {
    "I, A first": [R.one - R.a, R.a - R.ab, ssAB],
    "I, B first": [R.b - R.ab, R.one - R.b, ssAB],
    "II": [R.b - R.ab, R.a - R.ab, ssAB],
    "III": [R.noA - R.full, R.noB - R.full, ssAB]
  };
  const cell = ss => {
    const p = fPvalue(ss / mse, 1, dfe);
    const txt = `${ss.toFixed(1)} <span style="color:#5c6b63">(p ${p < 0.001 ? "< 0.001" : "= " + p.toFixed(3)})</span>`;
    return p < 0.05 ? `<b>${txt}</b>` : txt;
  };
  const head = Object.keys(table).map(k => `<th>${k}</th>`).join("");
  const body = ["A", "B", "A × B"].map((term, r) =>
    `<tr><td><b>${term}</b></td>${Object.values(table).map(v => `<td>${cell(v[r])}</td>`).join("")}</tr>`).join("");
  const means = [];
  for (const a of [-1, 1]) for (const b of [-1, 1]) {
    const ys = rows.filter(d => d.a === a && d.b === b).map(d => d.y);
    means.push({A: a < 0 ? "a1" : "a2", B: b < 0 ? "b1" : "b2", y: d3.mean(ys), n: ys.length});
  }
  const plot = Plot.plot({
    width: 300, height: 230, marginLeft: 40, style: {fontSize: "14px"},
    x: {label: "Factor A", domain: ["a1", "a2"]}, y: {label: "Cell mean", grid: true},
    color: {domain: ["b1", "b2"], range: ["#1d4e89", "#c45c26"], legend: true},
    marks: [
      Plot.line(means, {x: "A", y: "y", stroke: "B", strokeWidth: 2}),
      Plot.dot(means, {x: "A", y: "y", fill: "B", r: d => 3 + d.n / 3}),
      Plot.text(means, {x: "A", y: "y", text: d => `n = ${d.n}`, dx: 30, dy: d => d.B === "b1" ? 12 : -12, fontSize: 12})
    ]
  });
  return html`<div style="display:flex;gap:1.2em;align-items:flex-start">
    <div>${plot}</div>
    <div><table class="ojs-types"><thead><tr><th>Sum of squares</th>${head}</tr></thead>
    <tbody>${body}</tbody></table>
    <p style="font-size:14px;margin-top:0.4em">${N} rows, residual df ${dfe}. Bold: p &lt; 0.05.</p></div>
  </div>`;
}
```

::: {.notes}
A two-by-two design simulated in the browser; the imbalance puts more rows on the diagonal cells, which correlates A with B. Start with imbalance 0: the four columns agree. Raise it: Type I changes with the order, and Type II and III part ways once the interaction is non-zero. Set the interaction to zero and Type II equals Type III for the main effects. The point sizes are the cell sizes.
:::

## Generalised linear models {.center .pitfall-divider background-gradient="linear-gradient(160deg, #f7f4ef 0%, #d5eadf 100%)"}

## Favour the model, not a pretest

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 10
%%| fig-height: 2.8
flowchart LR
  question["Question"]
  support["Support of $$Y$$"]
  family["$$Y \mid x \sim \mathrm{family}(\mu)$$"]
  check["Residual plot"]
  report["Estimate and interval"]
  question --> support --> family --> check --> report
```

A [pretest]{.mark} that switches you from a $t$-test to a rank test still does not estimate $\mu = \mathbb{E}(Y \mid x)$. Rank tests answer a different contrast, and they have assumptions of their own.

The teaching sequence for the three models follows the SIB day on logistic regression and GLMs ([course](https://www.sib.swiss/training/course/20260907_ADDMG)). 📝 [Day 2, logistic regression and GLMs](references/day2-logistic-regression-and-glm-2026.pdf). 📝 [Day 1a, linear models](references/day1a-linear-regression-and-beyond-2026.pdf), is the hour before that sequence.

::: {.notes}
Walk the Mermaid: question → support → family → residual plot → estimate. Pretest switching $t$ to ranks still misses $\mu$. SIB day link is for students who want the full logistic/GLM course—optional aside.
:::

## The main GLMs share one skeleton {.smaller #sec-family-table}

Each model keeps $Y$ on its support and changes the [family]{.mark}; all of them are the [same skeleton](#sec-skeleton) with a different family and link.

| Support of $Y$ | Family, link | $\mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x)$ | Introduced on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Continuous, unrestricted | Gaussian, identity | $\sigma^2$ | [a continuous response](#sec-glm-gaussian) |
| Non-negative count | Poisson, log | $\mu$ | [a count, on the log](#sec-glm-poisson) |
| Count with extra variance | Negative binomial, log | $\mu + \mu^2/\theta$ | [negative binomial](#sec-nb-theta) |
| 0/1, or a proportion | Bernoulli or binomial, logit | $\pi(1 - \pi)$ | [a binary response](#sec-glm-bernoulli) |

The variance column is the [variance function]{.mark} $\phi V(\mu)$: the spread travels with the mean, except in the Gaussian row.

::: {.notes}
One row per model family of the afternoon, with the slide where each is introduced. The variance column is the part a transformation cannot reproduce: it is a property of the family, not a fix applied to the residuals afterwards.

**Going further.** In an exponential dispersion family the variance function $V(\mu) = b''\{(b')^{-1}(\mu)\}$ determines the family within the natural exponential families. Morris (*Annals of Statistics*, 1982) shows that exactly six have a quadratic $V$: Gaussian, Poisson, gamma, binomial, negative binomial, and the generalised hyperbolic secant. The Tweedie class, $V(\mu) = \mu^p$, interpolates: $p = 0$ Gaussian, $p = 1$ Poisson, $p = 2$ gamma, and $1 < p < 2$ a compound Poisson–gamma with exact zeros. The negative binomial NB2 is an exponential dispersion family only when $\theta$ is fixed, so `MASS::glm.nb` alternates between $\boldsymbol\beta$ and $\theta$.
:::

## One skeleton for every GLM :link: {#sec-skeleton}

```{.tikz}
%%| filename: dag-glm-skeleton
%%| alt: Plate diagram of a generalised linear model over rows i: the constant x i and the coefficients beta feed the dotted linear predictor eta i, which gives the dotted mean mu i through the inverse link, which gives the observed Y i through the family.
%%| width: 92%
\begin{tikzpicture}
\node[const] (x) {$x_i$};
\node[det, right=14mm of x] (eta) {$\eta_i$};
\node[det, right=14mm of eta] (mu) {$\mu_i$};
\node[obs, right=14mm of mu] (y) {$Y_i$};
\node[const, above=9mm of eta] (b) {$\boldsymbol\beta$};
\draw[edge] (x) -- (eta); \draw[edge] (b) -- (eta);
\draw[edge] (eta) -- (mu); \draw[edge] (mu) -- (y);
\node[note, below=2mm of eta] (n1) {$\eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i$};
\node[note, below=2mm of mu] (n2) {$\mu_i = g^{-1}(\eta_i)$};
\node[note, below=2mm of y] (n3) {$Y_i \sim \mathrm{family}(\mu_i)$};

\plate{p}{(x)(eta)(mu)(y)(n1)(n2)(n3)}{$i = 1,\ldots,n$}
\end{tikzpicture}
```

- **Family:** how $\mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x)$ depends on $\mu$
- **Link** $g$: the scale on which $\beta_1 x$ is linear
- **Mean** $\mu = \mathbb{E}(Y \mid x)$: what $\beta$ describes, after you invert $g$

Agresti is the reference for the theory and the worked models [@agrestiFoundationsLinearGeneralized2015]. Estimation is by [maximum likelihood]{.mark}, not by a normal test of $Y$. The letters are fixed on the [notation](#sec-notation) slide.

::: {.notes}
Read the graph left to right: $x_i$ and $\boldsymbol\beta$ give $\eta_i$, the inverse link gives $\mu_i$, the family gives $Y_i$. Three bullets map to variance structure, scale of $\beta$, and mean after inversion. Agresti citation is the theory anchor; MLE not normal test on raw $Y$.

**Going further.** Each family here is a one-parameter exponential family, $f(y;\theta,\phi) = \exp\{[y\theta - b(\theta)]/a(\phi) + c(y,\phi)\}$, so $\mu = b'(\theta)$ and $\mathrm{Var}(Y) = a(\phi)\,b''(\theta) = \phi V(\mu)$: the variance function $V$ is what "family" means on this slide. The canonical link is $g = (b')^{-1}$, which gives the identity, the logit and the log for the Gaussian, Bernoulli and Poisson. With the canonical link, $\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{y}$ is sufficient for $\boldsymbol\beta$ and the score equations reduce to $\mathbf{X}^{\top}(\mathbf{y}-\boldsymbol\mu) = \mathbf{0}$. Nelder and Wedderburn's 1972 paper unified the three cases; McCullagh and Nelder's *Generalized Linear Models* is the classical derivation, and Agresti the modern one [@agrestiFoundationsLinearGeneralized2015].
:::

## The link stays on the mean {.smaller #sec-glm-versus-transform}

$$
\underbrace{\mathbb{E}\{g(Y) \mid x\} = \mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta}_{\text{transform } Y} \qquad \text{is not} \qquad \underbrace{g\{\mathbb{E}(Y \mid x)\} = \mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta}_{\text{GLM}}
$$

because $\mathbb{E}\{g(Y)\} \neq g\{\mathbb{E}(Y)\}$ for a nonlinear $g$. What the GLM keeps [@agrestiFoundationsLinearGeneralized2015]:

::: {.incremental}
- the fit describes $\mu$ on the [original scale]{.mark}: a probability, an expected count, a rate
- no $\log(Y + 1)$: zeros stay data, and $g^{-1}$ keeps $\mu$ in its range
- the variance follows the mean, $\phi V(\mu)$, instead of a constant on a transformed scale
- coefficients are rate or odds ratios, and an [offset](#sec-casys-offset) carries the sampling effort
- likelihood inference: deviance, likelihood-ratio tests, AIC
:::

::: {.notes}
Read the two equations and the "is not". Then step the five fragments. The first one is the estimand argument of the non-Gaussian block; the third is the variance-function column of the previous table; the fourth is what makes a Poisson coefficient a rate ratio per read. The transformation route models $\mathbb{E}\{\log Y \mid x\}$, and $\exp$ of it is a geometric mean, not $\mathbb{E}(Y \mid x)$.

**Going further.** If $\log Y \mid x \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta, \sigma^2)$, then $\mathbb{E}(Y \mid x) = \exp(\mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta + \sigma^2/2)$: back-transforming the fitted mean underestimates by the factor $e^{\sigma^2/2}$, and if $\sigma^2$ depends on $x$ even the ratio between groups is biased (Duan's smearing estimator is the nonparametric repair, *Journal of the American Statistical Association*, 1983). The GLM score equations $\sum_i (Y_i - \mu_i)\,\partial\mu_i/\partial\boldsymbol\beta \,/\, \{\phi V(\mu_i)\} = \mathbf{0}$ use the observed $Y_i$, zeros included, and stay consistent for $\boldsymbol\beta$ when only the mean model is right (Wedderburn's quasi-likelihood).
:::

## Coefficients read on the link scale {#sec-glm-coef-meaning}

The link is chosen so $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ answers a substantive question on the mean.

For $\log(\mu) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$,

$$
\frac{\mu(x+1)}{\mu(x)} = e^{\beta_1}.
$$

For a logit on $\pi$, $e^{\beta_1}$ is an [odds ratio]{.mark}. The goal is not to make a histogram look Gaussian. The goal is a coefficient that names an effect on $\mu$. The compact contrast is [the link stays on the mean](#sec-glm-versus-transform).

::: {.notes}
For $\log\mu=\beta_0+\beta_1 x$, $\mu(x+1)/\mu(x)=e^{\beta_1}$. Logit: $e^{\beta_1}$ is an odds ratio. Goal is substantive effect on $\mu$, not a pretty histogram.

**Going further.** Wald intervals are computed on the link scale, $\hat{\beta}_1 \pm 1.96\, \mathrm{SE}$, and then exponentiated, which keeps a ratio positive; profile-likelihood intervals (`confint()` on a `glm`) are more accurate in small samples. The odds ratio approximates the risk ratio only when $\pi$ is small. The odds ratio is also non-collapsible: adding a covariate unrelated to treatment can change it, even in a randomised trial, because the marginal and conditional odds ratios differ (Greenland, Robins, and Pearl, *Statistical Science*, 1999). A log-linear rate ratio is collapsible in that sense.
:::

## A continuous response, on the identity {#sec-glm-gaussian}

A continuous response goes to a linear regression. The drawing is Gaussian, and the link is the [identity]{.mark}, so $\mu$ and the linear predictor are the same number.

```{.tikz}
%%| filename: dag-glm-gaussian
%%| alt: Plate diagram of the Gaussian linear model: x i and beta give eta i, mu i equals eta i, and Y i is normal with mean mu i and variance sigma squared, a constant.
%%| width: 92%
\begin{tikzpicture}
\node[const] (x) {$x_i$};
\node[det, right=14mm of x] (eta) {$\eta_i$};
\node[det, right=14mm of eta] (mu) {$\mu_i$};
\node[obs, right=14mm of mu] (y) {$Y_i$};
\node[const, above=9mm of eta] (b) {$\boldsymbol\beta$};
\draw[edge] (x) -- (eta); \draw[edge] (b) -- (eta);
\draw[edge] (eta) -- (mu); \draw[edge] (mu) -- (y);
\node[note, below=2mm of eta] (n1) {$\eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i$};
\node[note, below=2mm of mu] (n2) {$\mu_i = \eta_i$};
\node[note, below=2mm of y] (n3) {$Y_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_i, \sigma^2)$};
\node[const, above=9mm of y] (s) {$\sigma^2$}; \draw[edge] (s) -- (y);
\plate{p}{(x)(eta)(mu)(y)(n1)(n2)(n3)}{$i = 1,\ldots,n$}
\end{tikzpicture}
```

::: {.notes}
Identity link: $\mu=\eta$. The graph ends at Normal$(\mu,\sigma^2)$, with $\sigma^2$ a constant. This is linear regression dressed in GLM notation—bridge for students who only know `lm`.
:::

## What $\sigma$ does to a Gaussian {#sec-density-gaussian}

![Three normal densities. Widening sigma flattens the curve. Shifting the mean moves it.](figures/generated/density-gaussian.png){fig-alt="Three normal density curves. One has mean 0 and standard deviation 1. One has mean 0 and standard deviation 2 and is flatter. One has mean 1.5 and standard deviation 1." width="88%"}

These are the density functions, not a sample and not CA-SYS. $\sigma$ changes the spread. The mean shifts the curve. The two parameters are separate, which is the Gaussian case the [variance function](#sec-family-table) gives up.

::: {.notes}
Point at the flat red curve first: same mean, larger $\sigma$. Then the blue shift. Illustrative densities from `scripts/generate-density-curves.R`. Twenty seconds.
:::

## The fit maximises the likelihood {#sec-glm-mle}

The fit is by maximum likelihood. For a Gaussian linear model that maximiser is the least-squares fit. For the logit and the Poisson log link there is no closed form: the estimates come from an [iterative algorithm]{.mark}.

The Newton step for the logit, from the chapter embedded [below](#sec-burakov), uses the Bernoulli variances as weights:

$$
\boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t+1)} = \boldsymbol{\beta}^{(t)} + (\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}^{(t)}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^{\top}(\mathbf{y} - \boldsymbol{\pi}^{(t)}),
\qquad w_i = \pi_i(1-\pi_i).
$$

::: {.notes}
The course notes state that the maximiser is iterative and do not write the update. The displayed step is Burakov's equation (2.87), in the chapter embedded later. $\mathbf{W}$ is diagonal. At convergence, $(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X})^{-1}$ is the estimated covariance of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$.

**Going further.** The general algorithm is iteratively reweighted least squares: regress the working response $z_i = \eta_i + (y_i-\mu_i)\,g'(\mu_i)$ on $\mathbf{X}$ with weights $w_i = 1/\{V(\mu_i)\,g'(\mu_i)^2\}$, and repeat. This is Fisher scoring; with the canonical link the observed and expected information coincide, so it is also Newton–Raphson, and for the logit $w_i = \pi_i(1-\pi_i)$ as on the slide. Under regularity conditions (fixed $p$, information growing with $n$, true value inside the parameter space), $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ is consistent and approximately $\mathrm{Normal}\{\boldsymbol\beta, \phi(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X})^{-1}\}$. The maximiser need not exist: for a logit under separation the likelihood increases without bound, the failure on the checks figure. McCullagh and Nelder's *Generalized Linear Models* gives the derivation.
:::

## Three residual scales {#sec-glm-resid}

Three residuals are worth plotting after a GLM.

::: {.incremental}
- A [deviance residual]{.mark}, plotted against the fitted value and against each covariate. A curve is a missing piece of the linear predictor.

- A [Pearson residual]{.mark}, $(Y - \mu)$ divided by the fitted standard deviation. A trend against a covariate is a term the model does not yet contain.

- A [quantile residual]{.mark}. Under the fitted family it is uniform on $(0,1)$. A QQ plot against normal quantiles is the picture. Extra-large tails are a signal to leave the Poisson for a quasi-Poisson or a negative binomial.
:::


`acf()` is a quick check that the observations are not ordered in a way the independence assumption forbids. The Poisson simulation later draws the quantile residual for that family.

::: {.notes}
Step deviance, Pearson, quantile residuals and what curve each catches. Quantile residuals uniform under the fitted family—QQ against normal is the plot. `acf()` flags ordered dependence.

**Going further.** With $d_i$ the contribution of observation $i$ to the deviance, the deviance residual is $\mathrm{sign}(y_i-\hat\mu_i)\sqrt{d_i}$ and the Pearson residual is $(y_i-\hat\mu_i)/\sqrt{\hat\phi\,V(\hat\mu_i)}$. Both are only approximately normal, and for binary data or small counts they fall in bands, one per observed value, so a residual-against-fitted plot shows stripes whatever the model. The quantile residual is Dunn and Smyth's (1996, *Randomized quantile residuals*, *Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics*): $r_i = \Phi^{-1}(u_i)$, with $u_i$ uniform between $F(y_i^-;\hat\mu_i)$ and $F(y_i;\hat\mu_i)$. If the model is correct and its parameters known, the $r_i$ are exactly independent standard normal; with estimated parameters this holds asymptotically. The `DHARMa` package builds the same residual by simulating from the fitted model, which also covers mixed models.
:::

## Poisson regression {.center .pitfall-divider background-gradient="linear-gradient(160deg, #f7f4ef 0%, #d4efe8 100%)"}

## A count, on the log {#sec-glm-poisson}

A count goes to a [Poisson regression]{.mark}. The mean is often written as $\lambda$. That symbol is $\mu$ on these slides. The log link keeps $\mu > 0$, and $\exp(\beta_1)$ is a multiplicative change in the mean count.

```{.tikz}
%%| filename: dag-glm-poisson
%%| alt: Plate diagram of the Poisson regression: x i and beta give eta i, mu i is the exponential of eta i, and Y i is Poisson with mean mu i.
%%| width: 92%
\begin{tikzpicture}
\node[const] (x) {$x_i$};
\node[det, right=14mm of x] (eta) {$\eta_i$};
\node[det, right=14mm of eta] (mu) {$\mu_i$};
\node[obs, right=14mm of mu] (y) {$Y_i$};
\node[const, above=9mm of eta] (b) {$\boldsymbol\beta$};
\draw[edge] (x) -- (eta); \draw[edge] (b) -- (eta);
\draw[edge] (eta) -- (mu); \draw[edge] (mu) -- (y);
\node[note, below=2mm of eta] (n1) {$\eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i$};
\node[note, below=2mm of mu] (n2) {$\mu_i = e^{\eta_i}$};
\node[note, below=2mm of y] (n3) {$Y_i \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\mu_i)$};

\plate{p}{(x)(eta)(mu)(y)(n1)(n2)(n3)}{$i = 1,\ldots,n$}
\end{tikzpicture}
```

Four working assumptions: $Y$ is a count per unit of time or space; $\log \mu$ is linear in $x$; the observations are independent; and $\mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x) = \mu$. 📝 StatHarbor, [*Count data models*](references/count-data-models.pdf).

::: {.notes}
$\lambda$ on the slide is $\mu$ here; $\exp(\beta_1)$ multiplies mean count. Four assumptions at the bottom—especially $\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid x)=\mu$—are what CA-SYS will break.

**Going further.** Under the log link the Poisson log-likelihood is $\sum_i (y_i\eta_i - e^{\eta_i})$ up to a constant, so the score is $\mathbf{X}^{\top}(\mathbf{y}-\boldsymbol\mu)$ and, with an intercept, the fitted counts add up to the observed total; a factor covariate reproduces each group total exactly. The estimator of $\boldsymbol\beta$ stays consistent when the counts are not Poisson, provided $\log\mu$ is correctly specified: this is the pseudo-maximum-likelihood result of Gourieroux, Monfort and Trognon (1984, *Econometrica*). What breaks is the standard error, which relies on $\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid x)=\mu$; a sandwich estimator or a variance model repairs it (Cameron and Trivedi, *Regression Analysis of Count Data*).
:::

## What $\lambda$ does to a Poisson {#sec-density-poisson}

![Poisson probabilities for lambda 2, 8, and 20.](figures/generated/density-poisson.png){fig-alt="Three Poisson probability plots. Lambda 2 is piled near zero. Lambda 8 is wider. Lambda 20 is wider still and shifted right. The spread grows with the mean." width="88%"}

$\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \lambda = \mathbb{E}(Y)$. A larger mean is a wider plot. Illustrative probabilities from `scripts/generate-density-curves.R`, not a soil count.

::: {.notes}
The right-hand comb is both higher and wider. That is the one-parameter constraint. If their counts are wider than this picture, the next family is the negative binomial.
:::

## A table of counts is a log-linear model {#sec-loglinear}

[Penn State STAT 504, Lesson 10](https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat504/Lesson10) models a contingency table by a Poisson GLM. The cell count is $Y_{ab} \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\mu_{ab})$. The lesson is this [log-linear model]{.mark}. Independence, with neither margin as the response, is

$$
\log \mu_{ab} = \alpha + \alpha_a + \alpha_b.
$$

::: {.notes}
$Y_{ab}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(\mu_{ab})$; independence $\log\mu_{ab}=\alpha+\alpha_a+\alpha_b$. PSU STAT 504 lesson—joint model, not logit of one margin.

**Going further.** Independent Poisson cell counts, conditioned on their total $n$, are multinomial, and Birch (1963, *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B*) showed that a Poisson log-linear model with an intercept gives the same maximum-likelihood fitted counts as the multinomial, or as product-multinomial sampling when the fixed margins are in the model. That is why a Poisson `glm` can fit a contingency table whatever the sampling plan. The residual deviance of the independence model is the likelihood-ratio $G^2$ on $(A-1)(B-1)$ degrees of freedom for an $A \times B$ table, asymptotically equivalent to Pearson's $X^2$. Bishop, Fienberg and Holland's *Discrete Multivariate Analysis* develops the hierarchy of log-linear models.
:::

## Poisson · when the count matches the story {auto-animate=true}

Use it when $Y$ is a non-negative integer and, to a first approximation, $\mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x) = \mu$.

::: {data-id="pois-eq"}
$$
\log \mu = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x.
$$
:::

Colony counts on a plate are the clean case. Sequence reads are a count too, but with two complications: the [sampling effort]{.mark} differs between samples, and the counts are more variable than a Poisson.

::: {.notes}
$\log\mu=\beta_0+\beta_1 x$ with data-id animate. Colony counts are clean; reads need offset and extra variance—foreshadow CA-SYS. Var equals mean is the assumption to test first.
:::

## Poisson · the CA-SYS version {auto-animate=true}

::: {data-id="pois-eq"}
$$
\log \mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \mathrm{tilled}_i + \mathrm{year}_i + \log(\text{library size}_i).
$$
:::

$Y$ is the number of *Nitrospira* reads in a sample: a nitrite-oxidising genus, 153,771 reads across the 595 samples. The last term is the [offset](#sec-casys-offset), so $\beta_1$ is a ratio of rates per read.

::: {.notes}
Point out that the equation changed in two places from the previous slide: year entered as a factor, and the offset appeared. Neither is cosmetic. Without the offset, a sample sequenced twice as deeply looks twice as rich in Nitrospira.
:::

## Poisson · the call {#sec-casys-poisson-code}

::: {.codewindow .r}
poisson-dispersion.R
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
casys <- read.csv("data/derived/casys_teaching.csv")

fit_pois <- glm(
  nitrospira_reads ~ tillage + factor(year) + offset(log(total_reads)),
  family = poisson,
  data = casys
)

# Is one parameter doing both jobs?
sum(residuals(fit_pois, "pearson")^2) / fit_pois$df.residual
#> 10.6
```
:::

A Poisson sets $\mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x) = \mu$. A [Pearson statistic]{.mark} of 10.6 per degree of freedom says the data are about ten times more variable than that.

::: {.notes}
Run this if the laptop allows. The dispersion statistic is the number to look at before reading any coefficient, because the coefficient will look fine and the standard error will not. The rule of thumb is that a value near 1 is consistent with the Poisson; 10.6 is not a borderline case.

**Going further.** The statistic is the moment estimator of the dispersion, $\hat\phi = X^2/(n-p)$ with $X^2 = \sum_i (y_i-\hat\mu_i)^2/V(\hat\mu_i)$; under a correct Poisson model $X^2$ is approximately $\chi^2_{n-p}$, so $\hat\phi$ is near 1. The quasi-Poisson fit keeps the Poisson estimates and multiplies every standard error by $\sqrt{\hat\phi}$; here $\sqrt{10.6} \approx 3.3$, close to the threefold widening the negative binomial gives a few slides on. The deviance-based estimate $D/(n-p)$ is less reliable when many $\hat\mu_i$ are small, which is why McCullagh and Nelder prefer the Pearson form. A formal check is the score test of Dean and Lawless (1989, *Journal of the American Statistical Association*).
:::

## The count measures a latent share {#sec-measure}

[Sarkar and Stephens](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41588-021-00873-4) separate a [measurement model]{.mark} from a model for the latent intensity. The paper is about genes in single cells. The same split applies to any feature counted inside a sample of finite depth: a taxon, a transcript, a fragment.

Let $s_i$ be the [library size]{.mark}, the total count in sample $i$, and let $\lambda_{i\ell}$ be the relative intensity of feature $\ell$, a share of that sample. The measurement model is

$$
Y_{i\ell} \mid s_i, \lambda_{i\ell} \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(s_i \lambda_{i\ell}).
$$

Dividing by the depth is this rate: the offset $\log s_i$, with its coefficient fixed at 1. A coefficient $e^{\beta}$ is then a ratio of [rates per read]{.mark}, not of raw counts.

::: {.notes}
$Y_{i\ell}\mid s_i,\lambda_{i\ell}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(s_i\lambda_{i\ell})$; offset $\log s_i$ with coefficient 1. Sarkar–Stephens single-cell paper, same logic for any feature in finite depth.

**Going further.** An offset is a covariate whose coefficient is fixed at 1: $\log\mu_i = \log s_i + \mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta$ is $\mu_i/s_i = \exp(\mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta)$, so $\boldsymbol\beta$ acts on the rate per read. Entering $\log s_i$ as an ordinary covariate and testing its slope against 1 checks that proportionality. Modelling $y_i/s_i$ with a Gaussian model is not equivalent: it discards the fact that the variance of a proportion falls with depth.
