Differential-abundance software often replaces the raw library size by a robust size factor, such as the median-of-ratios of Anders and Huber (2010, *Genome Biology*), because a few dominant features can distort the total.
:::

## The measurement drawing {#sec-measure-dag}

```{.tikz}
%%| filename: dag-measurement
%%| alt: Plate diagram of the measurement layer: inside a plate over samples i sits the size factor s i, a constant; inside a nested plate over features l sit the latent share lambda i l, the dotted mean mu i l equal to s i times lambda i l, and the observed count Y i l.
%%| width: 80%
\begin{tikzpicture}
\node[stoch] (lam) {$\lambda_{i\ell}$};
\node[det, right=14mm of lam] (mu) {$\mu_{i\ell}$};
\node[obs, right=14mm of mu] (y) {$Y_{i\ell}$};
\node[const, above=13mm of mu] (s) {$s_i$};
\draw[edge] (lam) -- (mu); \draw[edge] (s) -- (mu); \draw[edge] (mu) -- (y);
\node[note, below=2mm of mu] (n2) {$\mu_{i\ell} = s_i\lambda_{i\ell}$};
\node[note, below=2mm of y] (n3) {$\mathrm{Poisson}(\mu_{i\ell})$};
\plate{pl}{(lam)(mu)(y)(n2)(n3)}{$\ell$: feature}
\plate{pi}{(s)(pl)(pl-lab)}{$i$: sample}
\end{tikzpicture}
```

Library size and relative intensity meet in the Poisson mean. The sctransform slides fit this regression, with the slope of $\log s_i$ fixed.

::: {.notes}
Graph: $\lambda$ and $s$ meet in the dotted node $\mu=s\lambda$, then the Poisson draw. Pearson-residual figure below is this regression with fixed log-depth slope.
:::

## The Poisson measurement model, as a theorem {#sec-box1}

::: {#thm-poisson-measurement name="Poisson measurement model, Sarkar and Stephens (Box 1)"}
In sample $i$, suppose that every molecule is equally likely to be observed, that molecules are observed independently, and that only a small share of them is observed. Then
$$
Y_{i\ell} \mid s_i, \lambda_{i\ell} \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(s_i\lambda_{i\ell}),
$$
and the depth $s_i$ enters the regression as the offset $\log s_i$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="When to use it"}
The last two conditions are usually plausible: they cite 10–20% capture in single-cell data. The first fails when stability, location, or sequence changes the chance that a molecule is seen; a bias that varies between samples makes the measurement [negative binomial](#sec-nb-theta).
:::

::: {.notes}
The three conditions are Box 1 of Sarkar and Stephens. The result is the law of rare events: many molecules, each captured independently with a small probability, give a binomial count close to a Poisson. A bias that is shared across samples can enter the Poisson model as a covariate; one that changes from sample to sample is extra noise. If a later protocol observes a larger share of the molecules, the measurement variance falls below the Poisson's.

**Going further.** If sample $i$ contains $M_{i\ell}$ molecules of feature $\ell$ and each is captured independently with probability $p_i$, then $Y_{i\ell} \mid M_{i\ell} \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(M_{i\ell}, p_i)$, and as $p_i \to 0$ with $M_{i\ell}p_i$ fixed this tends to $\mathrm{Poisson}(M_{i\ell}p_i)$; writing $M_{i\ell}p_i = s_i\lambda_{i\ell}$ separates the depth from the relative intensity. If the capture probability itself varies, $p_i \sim$ Beta or $\lambda$ varies between samples, integrating it out gives an overdispersed margin, the negative binomial for a gamma mixing law.
:::

## Negative binomial regression {.center .pitfall-divider background-gradient="linear-gradient(160deg, #f7f4ef 0%, #e4d8f5 100%)"}

## Negative binomial · two parameters, one hierarchy {.dag-large #sec-nb-theta}

Keep the log link for the mean $\mu$; add a [dispersion]{.mark} $\theta > 0$, the size in `MASS::glm.nb`. The count is a Poisson whose rate is itself a gamma draw.

```{.tikz}
%%| filename: dag-glm-negbin
%%| alt: Plate diagram of the negative binomial regression over rows i. The constant x i and the coefficients beta give the dotted mean mu i through the log link. The latent rate lambda i is drawn from a gamma distribution with mean mu i and shape theta, a constant. The observed count Y i is Poisson with mean lambda i.
\begin{tikzpicture}
\node[const] (x) {$x_i$};
\node[det, right=16mm of x] (mu) {$\mu_i$};
\node[stoch, right=24mm of mu] (lam) {$\lambda_i$};
\node[obs, right=24mm of lam] (y) {$Y_i$};
\node[const, above=9mm of mu] (b) {$\boldsymbol\beta$};
\node[const, above=9mm of lam] (th) {$\theta$};
\draw[edge] (x) -- (mu); \draw[edge] (b) -- (mu); \draw[edge] (mu) -- (lam);
\draw[edge] (th) -- (lam); \draw[edge] (lam) -- (y);
\node[note, below=2mm of mu] (n1) {$\log\mu_i = \mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol\beta$};
\node[note, below=2mm of lam] (n2) {$\lambda_i \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\theta, \theta/\mu_i)$};
\node[note, below=2mm of y] (n3) {$Y_i \mid \lambda_i \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_i)$};
\plate{p}{(x)(mu)(lam)(y)(n1)(n2)(n3)}{$i = 1,\ldots,n$}
\end{tikzpicture}
```

::: model
$$
\mathbb{E}(Y \mid x) = \mu, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x) = \mu + \frac{\mu^2}{\theta}.
$$
:::

::: {.notes}
Read the graph left to right: the mean comes from the linear predictor, the gamma draw lets each row have its own rate around that mean, and the Poisson is the counting. Large $\theta$ means a gamma concentrated on $\mu$, so the model returns to the Poisson. 📄 Townes reviews the count families in [*Review of probability distributions for modeling count data*](references/townes-count-distributions-2020.pdf). Stress that $\theta$ is not a second scientific effect to interpret.

**Going further.** With $\lambda \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\text{shape } \theta, \text{rate } \theta/\mu)$, integrating $\lambda$ out of $\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)$ gives $\Pr(Y=y) = \frac{\Gamma(y+\theta)}{\Gamma(\theta)\,y!}\left(\frac{\theta}{\theta+\mu}\right)^{\theta}\left(\frac{\mu}{\theta+\mu}\right)^{y}$, Cameron and Trivedi's NB2. NB1, $\mathrm{Var}(Y) = (1+\delta)\mu$, has the quasi-Poisson's shape and is a different model. Testing the Poisson against it puts $1/\theta = 0$ on the boundary of the parameter space, so the likelihood-ratio statistic is a 50:50 mixture of $\chi^2_0$ and $\chi^2_1$ and the naive $p$-value should be halved (Self and Liang, 1987, *Journal of the American Statistical Association*).
:::

## Two sources of variance {#sec-nb-two-variances}

$$
\mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x) = \underbrace{\mu}_{\text{technical: Poisson counting}} + \underbrace{\mu^2/\theta}_{\text{biological: } \lambda \text{ varies between units}}
$$

Divided by $\mu^2$, the squared coefficient of variation splits the same way:

$$
\mathrm{CV}^2 = \frac{1}{\mu} + \frac{1}{\theta}.
$$

Deeper sampling raises $\mu$ and shrinks the [technical]{.mark} term. The [biological]{.mark} floor $1/\theta$ stays, however many reads you buy.

::: {.notes}
This is the reading that makes $\theta$ useful. The Poisson part is the noise any counting process has; the quadratic part is the heterogeneity of the true rate between samples, enclosures, or cells. A Poisson dispersion statistic of 10.6 on CA-SYS says the second term dominates. In sequencing, $\sqrt{1/\theta}$ is the biological coefficient of variation of edgeR (McCarthy, Chen and Smyth, *Nucleic Acids Research*, 2012).

**Going further.** The decomposition is the law of total variance of the next slide, read on the coefficient-of-variation scale: $\mathrm{CV}^2(Y) = \mathbb{E}\{\mathrm{Var}(Y \mid \lambda)\}/\mu^2 + \mathrm{Var}(\lambda)/\mu^2$. A design consequence follows: once $\mu \gg \theta$, more depth barely changes the precision, and more biological replicates are the only way to shrink the variance of a group mean.
:::

## The variance, by the tower rule {#sec-tower}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="64%"}
$Y \mid \lambda \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)$, with $\mathbb{E}(\lambda) = \mu$ and $\mathrm{Var}(\lambda) = \mu^2/\theta$ for the gamma.

$$
\mathbb{E}(Y) = \mathbb{E}\{\mathbb{E}(Y \mid \lambda)\} = \mathbb{E}(\lambda) = \mu
$$

$$
\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}\{\mathrm{Var}(Y \mid \lambda)\}}_{\mathbb{E}(\lambda) \,=\, \mu} + \underbrace{\mathrm{Var}\{\mathbb{E}(Y \mid \lambda)\}}_{\mathrm{Var}(\lambda) \,=\, \mu^2/\theta}
$$
:::
::: {.column width="36%"}
![](figures/generated/sketch-nongauss-b-gamma-poisson.png){.sketch fig-alt="Hand-drawn violet gamma curve for lambda with three coloured draws; each draw feeds a narrow Poisson bump at its own place, and together they make one wide black bump labelled NB."}
:::
::::

The [law of total variance]{.mark} gives the negative-binomial variance without writing its probability function: a Poisson–gamma compound.

::: {.notes}
Two lines, both from conditioning on the latent rate. The Poisson contributes its mean as variance; the gamma contributes its own variance. McCullagh and Nelder write the extra term $\mu^2/\alpha$; the alternative form $\mu + \alpha\mu^2$ returns the Poisson as $\alpha \to 0$.

**Going further.** The law of total variance, $\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \mathbb{E}\{\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid\lambda)\} + \mathrm{Var}\{\mathbb{E}(Y\mid\lambda)\}$, holds for any latent $\lambda$ with finite variance, so every Poisson mixture is overdispersed: $\mathrm{Var}(Y) \geq \mathbb{E}(Y)$, with equality only when $\lambda$ is constant. A log-normal $\lambda$ with $\log\lambda \sim \mathrm{Normal}(m, \sigma^2)$ gives $\mathrm{Var}(\lambda) = \mu^2(e^{\sigma^2}-1)$, the same quadratic shape with heavier tails: the Poisson log-normal. Greenwood and Yule (1920, *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society*) introduced the gamma mixture for accident counts; Karlis and Xekalaki (2005, *International Statistical Review*) review mixed Poisson distributions.
:::

## Same mean, three values of $\theta$ {#sec-density-nb}

![Negative binomial probabilities at mean 8 for theta 1, 5, and 50, with the Poisson of the same mean.](figures/generated/density-negbin.png){fig-alt="Probability plots at mean 8. Theta 1 is the widest, with a long right tail. Theta 50 sits close to the Poisson of the same mean." width="88%"}

The mean stays 8. Small $\theta$ puts more mass in the tail, because $\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \mu + \mu^2/\theta$. Large $\theta$ collapses toward the Poisson. Illustrative, from `scripts/generate-density-curves.R`.

::: {.notes}
Cover the grey Poisson last. Ask which $\theta$ matches a Pearson dispersion near 1. The answer is the large one. The CA-SYS $\hat\theta$ of 29 is in that direction, not at 1.
:::

## One mean, two variance assumptions {#sec-casys-nb}

![Rate ratio for tilled against no-till, with a Poisson interval and a much wider negative binomial interval.](figures/generated/casys-poisson-vs-nb.png){fig-alt="Two horizontal intervals for the same rate ratio of about 0.97. The Poisson interval spans roughly 0.962 to 0.982; the negative binomial interval spans 0.941 to 1.002 and crosses one." width="94%"}

| Family | Rate ratio | 95% interval |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Poisson | 0.972 | 0.962 to 0.982 |
| Negative binomial | 0.971 | 0.941 to 1.002 |

::: {.notes}
This is the slide to slow down on. The point estimate barely moves, 0.972 against 0.971, because both models use the same mean equation. The interval is 3.1 times wider. Under the Poisson the contrast is "detected"; under the negative binomial it crosses one. Nothing about the biology changed between the two rows, only an assumption about the variance. Ask the room which interval they would put in a paper.

**Going further.** The near-identical point estimates are expected: when $\log\mu$ is correctly specified, the Poisson score equations give a consistent $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ whatever the true variance (Gourieroux, Monfort and Trognon, 1984), and the negative binomial only re-weights observations, by $\mu_i/(1+\mu_i/\theta)$ instead of $\mu_i$. The two fits therefore differ in efficiency and, mostly, in the covariance matrix. A third option keeps the Poisson estimate with a sandwich covariance, valid under any variance function but less stable in small samples (`sandwich` package). Ver Hoef and Boveng (2007, *Ecology*) compare quasi-Poisson and negative-binomial weighting and suggest plotting binned squared residuals against $\hat\mu$ to choose between a linear and a quadratic variance.
:::

## Read the mean, then $\theta$ {#sec-nb-read}

::: {.incremental}
- The rate ratio is a statement about $\mu$, on the log link, per read
- $\theta$ is not a second effect; it describes [leftover variation]{.mark}
- With the wider interval, 1.00 is compatible with these data
:::


A 2.9% lower rate under tillage would matter agronomically. These 595 samples cannot separate it from no difference.

::: {.notes}
The last line is the honest summary, and it is the pitfalls lesson applied to a real fit: the estimate is the result, and the interval says how much the data constrain it. Resist the temptation to call this a null finding. It is an imprecise estimate of a small contrast, which is a different sentence.
:::

## Same count, three implementations

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Poisson

$$
\log \mu = \mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta} + \log(\text{library size}), \qquad \mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x) = \mu.
$$

Tilled against no-till: rate ratio **0.972** (0.962 to 0.982). Pearson $\chi^2/\mathrm{df} = 10.6$, so that interval is too narrow.

### Negative binomial

$$
\mathrm{Var}(Y \mid x) = \mu + \mu^2/\theta, \qquad \hat\theta = 29.3.
$$

Same mean equation: rate ratio **0.971** (0.941 to 1.002). The interval is 3.1 times wider and crosses 1.

### $\log(Y+1)$, then Gaussian

$$
\mathbb{E}\{\log(Y+1) \mid x\} = \mathbf{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\beta}.
$$

That coefficient is not a rate ratio for $\mu$, and the library size no longer enters as an offset. The two means are not the same function of $x$.

:::

Arrow keys step the tabs. All three are fits to the CA-SYS reads, from [generate-data-figures.R](scripts/generate-data-figures.R), using [casys_teaching.csv](data/derived/casys_teaching.csv).

::: {.notes}
Tab through Poisson, NB, $\log(Y+1)$ Gaussian—arrow keys on slide. Rate ratio 0.972 vs 0.971, Pearson 10.6, $\hat\theta=29.3$, log-plus-one loses offset interpretation. Script path `generate-data-figures.R` if asked.
:::

## The observation model is the margin {#sec-obs-model}

An [expression model]{.mark} is a distribution $g_\ell$ for the latent share $\lambda_{i\ell}$. The [observation model]{.mark} is the distribution of $Y$ after $\lambda$ has been integrated out.

```{.tikz}
%%| filename: dag-observation-model
%%| alt: Plate diagram: a feature-level distribution g l, a constant, gives the latent rate lambda i l; lambda i l and the size factor s i give the observed count Y i l, Poisson with mean s i lambda i l. Integrating lambda out gives the margin of Y i l.
%%| width: 80%
\begin{tikzpicture}
\node[const] (g) {$g_\ell$};
\node[stoch, right=14mm of g] (lam) {$\lambda_{i\ell}$};
\node[obs, right=16mm of lam] (y) {$Y_{i\ell}$};
\node[const, above=12mm of y] (s) {$s_i$};
\draw[edge] (g) -- (lam); \draw[edge] (lam) -- (y); \draw[edge] (s) -- (y);
\node[note, below=2mm of y] (n3) {$\mathrm{Poisson}(s_i\lambda_{i\ell})$};
\node[note, below=2mm of lam] (n1) {$\lambda_{i\ell} \sim g_\ell$};
\plate{pl}{(lam)(y)(n1)(n3)}{$\ell$: feature}
\plate{pi}{(s)(pl)(pl-lab)}{$i$: sample}
\end{tikzpicture}
```

A gamma $g_\ell$ produces a negative-binomial margin. A point-gamma $g_\ell$, a spike at zero plus a gamma, produces a zero-inflated negative-binomial margin. The Poisson recommendation is for the measurement layer. The margin is usually wider, because the latent share varies across samples.

::: {.notes}
$g_\ell$ for latent $\lambda$; integrate to margin of $Y$. Gamma → NB margin; point-gamma → ZINB. Poisson recommendation is measurement layer; margin usually wider.
:::

## sctransform A · one negative binomial regression per gene {.dag-large #sec-sct-model}

```{.tikz}
%%| filename: dag-sctransform
%%| alt: Plate diagram of the sctransform model with two crossed plates. The plate over cells c holds the depth n c, a constant. The plate over genes g holds the intercept beta g 0 and the dispersion theta g, both constants. Where the plates cross sit the dotted mean mu g c and the observed count Y g c.
\begin{tikzpicture}
\node[det] (mu) {$\mu_{gc}$};
\node[obs, right=22mm of mu] (y) {$Y_{gc}$};
\node[const, above=11mm of mu] (n) {$n_c$};
\node[const, left=16mm of mu] (b0) {$\beta_{g0}$};
\node[const, right=16mm of y] (th) {$\theta_g$};
\draw[edge] (n) -- (mu); \draw[edge] (b0) -- (mu); \draw[edge] (mu) -- (y); \draw[edge] (th) -- (y);
\node[note, below=2mm of mu] (n1) {$\ln\mu_{gc} = \beta_{g0} + \ln n_c$};
\node[note, below=2mm of y] (n2) {$\mathrm{NB}(\mu_{gc}, \theta_g)$};
\plate{pc}{(n)(mu)(y)(n1)(n2)}{$c$: cell}
\plate{pg}{(b0)(th)(mu)(y)(n1)(n2)(pc-lab)}{$g$: gene}
\end{tikzpicture}
```

Each gene $g$ gets an intercept and a dispersion; each cell $c$ brings its [depth]{.mark} $n_c$, the total UMI count. 📄 Choudhary and Satija, [*Comparison and evaluation of statistical error models for scRNA-seq*](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13059-021-02584-9) (2022), describe version 2.

::: {.notes}
Genes and cells are crossed, not nested: every gene is counted in every cell, so the two plates overlap on $\mu_{gc}$ and $Y_{gc}$. The model has no covariate of interest: it is a normalisation model, and the Pearson residuals it returns are the input of the downstream analysis. The next three slides are its three steps, on a simulated matrix of 1,500 genes and 800 cells, seed `20261005`.

**Going further.** The original sctransform (Hafemeister and Satija, *Genome Biology*, 2019) fitted $\ln\mu_{gc} = \beta_{g0} + \beta_{g1}\log_{10} n_c$ with both coefficients regularised across genes. Lause, Berens and Kobak (*Genome Biology*, 2021) showed that the per-gene slope estimates were unstable and that the analytic value is 1 on the natural-log scale: version 2 sets $\beta_{g1} = \ln 10$ on $\log_{10} n_c$, which is the offset $\ln n_c$ on the slide, and keeps only the intercept and $\theta_g$ per gene.
:::

## sctransform B · depth enters as an offset {.fit-fig #sec-sct-offset}

![Two scatter plots for one abundant simulated gene. Left: log counts against log depth, with a line of slope 1. Right: log of count over fitted mean against log depth, flat around zero.](figures/generated/sct-offset.png){fig-alt="Left, orange points of the gene's log10 UMI count rise with log10 total UMI per cell, along a blue line of slope 1. Right, blue points of log10 count over fitted mean scatter around zero with no trend across depth." width="94%"}

The slope of $\ln n_c$ is fixed at 1, so only $\beta_{g0}$ is fitted. Doubling the depth doubles $\mu_{gc}$; what remains is the [rate per UMI]{.mark}, the same in a shallow and a deep cell.

::: {.notes}
Left: one abundant gene; its counts grow in proportion to the cell's depth. Right: dividing by the fitted mean removes that trend. With the slope fixed, the maximum-likelihood intercept has a closed form, $e^{\beta_{g0}} = \sum_c Y_{gc} / \sum_c n_c$, which is what the simulation uses. Illustrative, seed `20261005`.
:::

## sctransform C · Pearson residuals stabilise the variance {.fig-260 #sec-sct-pearson}

$$
r_{gc} = \frac{Y_{gc} - \hat\mu_{gc}}{\sqrt{\hat\mu_{gc} + \hat\mu_{gc}^2/\hat\theta_g}}
$$

![Two scatter plots over genes. Left: the variance of raw counts against the gene mean, rising far above the Poisson line. Right: the variance of Pearson residuals, near 1 for the negative binomial and rising for the Poisson.](figures/generated/sct-pearson.png){fig-alt="Left, orange points of raw count variance against gene mean on log scales rise steeply above a dashed Poisson line. Right, the variance of negative-binomial Pearson residuals stays near 1 across all gene means, while grey Poisson residuals rise above 3 for abundant genes." width="90%"}

Raw counts are [heteroscedastic]{.mark}; after dividing by the negative-binomial standard deviation, every gene has a variance near 1.

::: {.notes}
Left: the variance of the counts grows faster than the mean, the quadratic term. Right: the same genes after dividing by the fitted standard deviation. Grey is what a Poisson model would give: abundant genes keep variances of 3 to 10, which then dominate a principal-component analysis. Residuals are clipped at $\pm\sqrt{C}$, with $C$ the number of cells, as in sctransform.

**Going further.** A Pearson residual has mean 0 and variance 1 under the fitted model; residual variance above 1 for a gene is then evidence of biological variation beyond the model, which is how sctransform selects variable genes. Version 2 also bounds the standard deviation from below, so a gene seen once or twice does not produce an enormous residual (Choudhary and Satija, 2022). Lause and colleagues (2021) show that with a shared $\theta$ the residuals have a closed form and need no per-gene fit.
:::

## sctransform D · borrow $\theta$ across genes {.fit-fig #sec-sct-regularise}

![Per-gene maximum-likelihood estimates of theta against gene abundance, scattered widely for rare genes, with a loess trend rising with abundance.](figures/generated/sct-theta-regularisation.png){fig-alt="Grey points of estimated theta against geometric-mean abundance on log scales. They rise with abundance and scatter widely at low abundance. A purple loess curve runs through them, rising from about 0.15 to about 17." width="84%"}

A rare gene has too few counts to estimate its own $\theta_g$. The fit regresses the per-gene estimates on abundance with a [loess]{.mark} curve and uses the curve instead. That is [empirical Bayes]{.mark}: the prior is estimated from all the genes, then each gene borrows from it.

::: {.notes}
Version 2 leaves out genes with $\sigma^2 \le \mu$ or $\mu < 0.001$: they keep $\theta = \infty$, a Poisson. Empirical Bayes in one sentence: estimate the distribution that the gene-level parameters come from using the data of all genes, then treat it as the prior for each one. Here the prior is a curve, and every gene is pulled all the way onto it. The intercept is regularised the same way in sctransform; abundance is the geometric mean, which is less sensitive to a few outlying cells. The simulation leaves 72 genes without evidence of overdispersion, seed `20261005`.

**Going further.** In a full empirical-Bayes treatment each gene's estimate would be shrunk towards the trend by a weight that depends on its own precision, as DESeq2 does for its dispersion on the log scale (Love, Huber and Anders, *Genome Biology*, 2014) and edgeR with its weighted likelihood. sctransform's choice, replacing the estimate by the trend, is the limit of complete shrinkage; it is robust and fast, and it gives up any gene-specific dispersion that differs from genes of the same abundance. The trend is fitted on a subset of 2,000 genes sampled by abundance in the implementation.
:::

## Six count distributions, one map {.count-map #sec-count-map}

```{.tikz}
%%| filename: count-distribution-map
%%| alt: A map of six distributions. Top left Poisson, top right negative binomial, joined by an arrow labelled add overdispersion, lambda drawn from a gamma and integrated out, with a dashed arrow from a gamma node below saying it is the conjugate prior. Bottom left multinomial, bottom right Dirichlet-multinomial, joined by an arrow labelled pi drawn from a Dirichlet and integrated out, with a dashed arrow from a Dirichlet node. Vertical arrows condition on the total: Poisson to multinomial, negative binomial to Dirichlet-multinomial, and gamma to Dirichlet by normalising. Gamma and Dirichlet are shaded as continuous.
\begin{tikzpicture}[
  dist/.style={rectangle, rounded corners=4pt, draw=ink, fill=white, align=center, text width=42mm, minimum height=15mm, line width=0.9pt, font=\small},
  cont/.style={dist, draw=latdraw, fill=latfill},
  lab/.style={font=\footnotesize\itshape, text=ink!80, align=center},
  dashedge/.style={edge, dashed, draw=latdraw}]
\node[dist] (pois) at (0, 0) {\textbf{Poisson}$(\lambda)$\\ $\mathbb{E}(Y) = \mathrm{Var}(Y) = \lambda$};
\node[dist] (nb) at (11, 0) {\textbf{Negative binomial}$(\mu, \alpha)$\\ $\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \mu + \mu^2/\alpha$};
\node[cont] (gam) at (5.5, -2.6) {\textbf{Gamma}$(\alpha, \beta)$\\ continuous, positive};
\node[cont] (dir) at (5.5, -5.4) {\textbf{Dirichlet}$(\boldsymbol\alpha)$\\ continuous, on the simplex};
\node[dist] (mult) at (0, -8) {\textbf{Multinomial}$(m, \boldsymbol\pi)$\\ counts given their total};
\node[dist] (dm) at (11, -8) {\textbf{Dirichlet--multinomial}$(m, \boldsymbol\alpha)$\\ overdispersed composition};
\draw[edge] (pois) -- node[lab, above] {add overdispersion: $\lambda \sim$ Gamma,\\ integrate out} (nb);
\draw[dashedge] (gam) -- node[lab, right] {conjugate prior} (5.5, 0);
\draw[edge] (mult) -- node[lab, below] {add overdispersion: $\boldsymbol\pi \sim$ Dirichlet,\\ integrate out} (dm);
\draw[dashedge] (dir) -- node[lab, right] {conjugate prior} (5.5, -8);
\draw[edge] (pois) -- node[lab, left] {condition on\\ the total $m$} (mult);
\draw[edge] (nb) -- node[lab, right] {condition on\\ the total $m$\\ (shared scale)} (dm);
\draw[edge] (gam) -- node[lab, right] {normalise\\ independent gammas} (dir);
\end{tikzpicture}
```

Horizontal arrows integrate a continuous prior; vertical arrows condition on the total. Shaded nodes are the continuous members. Redrawn after 📄 [Townes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.04343).

::: {.notes}
Read the top row first: Poisson to negative binomial by a gamma rate, the derivation of the tower slide. Then the left column: independent Poissons given their sum are a multinomial, which is what a sequencing library does by fixing the depth. The right column repeats the step with overdispersion, and needs a shared scale parameter. The bottom row is the compositional version of the top one.

**Going further.** If $Y_\ell \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_\ell)$ independently and $m = \sum_\ell Y_\ell$, then $\mathbf{Y} \mid m \sim \mathrm{Multinomial}(m, \boldsymbol\pi)$ with $\pi_\ell = \lambda_\ell / \sum_k \lambda_k$, and the Poisson log-linear model with a sample intercept gives the same fitted proportions as the multinomial (Birch, 1963). Independent gammas with a common rate, divided by their sum, are Dirichlet; independent negative binomials with a shared scale, conditioned on their sum, are Dirichlet–multinomial. Shared shapes with different means do not stay in the family.
:::

## Compound, mixture, and the Tweedie line {visibility="visible"}

::: {.incremental}
- $\lambda$ fixed: $\mathrm{Var}(\lambda) = 0$, and $Y$ is Poisson.

- $\lambda$ continuous: a compound distribution. A gamma $\lambda$ is the negative binomial. A normal draw for $\log\lambda$ is the Poisson log-normal. Townes notes that this margin has a heavier tail than the negative binomial.

- The latent discrete: a mixture. The zero-inflated model is the spike at a structural zero plus a count distribution.
:::


Townes's Poisson–Tweedie has $\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \mu + \phi\mu^{p}$. The negative binomial is $p = 2$. These margins generally have no closed likelihood.

::: {.notes}
Step three fragments: fixed $\lambda$ Poisson; continuous $\lambda$ compound (gamma NB, log-normal heavier tail); discrete latent mixture including ZIP. Tweedie $\mathrm{Var}=\mu+\phi\mu^p$, $p=2$ is NB; often no closed likelihood.
:::

## Independent counts, given their sum {#sec-multinomial-sum visibility="visible"}

Townes's identity: independent Poisson counts, conditioned on their total, are one multinomial draw. If $Y_\ell \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_\ell)$ independently and $M = \sum Y_\ell$, then

$$
\mathbf{Y} \mid M \sim \mathrm{Multinomial}\!\left(M,\; \pi_\ell = \lambda_\ell \big/ \textstyle\sum_k \lambda_k\right).
$$

The same step with independent negative binomials that share a scale parameter returns a Dirichlet-multinomial. The shared scale is required. Negative binomials with a shared shape and different means do not, after conditioning, stay Dirichlet-multinomial.

A sequencing library is this conditioning. The Sarkar rate $s_i\lambda_{i\ell}$ is the Poisson layer. Given the library size, the vector of features is multinomial. Modelling the counts as independent Poissons with an offset, or as one multinomial, are the two sides of that identity.

::: {.notes}
Poisson conditioned on $M$ → multinomial with $\pi_\ell=\lambda_\ell/\sum\lambda$. NB with shared scale → Dirichlet-multinomial; differing shapes break that. Library size conditioning is the sequencing identity.
:::

## Other count models {.center .pitfall-divider background-gradient="linear-gradient(160deg, #f7f4ef 0%, #e4d8f5 100%)"}

## Poisson log-normal · a Gaussian latent on the log mean {.fit-fig #sec-pln}

![The Poisson log-normal model: counts and covariates enter a latent Gaussian layer, the counts are Poisson given the latent, and the same layer is constrained for a known grouping, a mixture, a low-rank covariance, or a sparse precision.](figures/sources/poisson-log-normal.webp){fig-alt="Standard Poisson log-normal. Counts Y and covariates X enter a latent Z drawn normal with mean mu and covariance Sigma. Given Z, the counts are Poisson with mean exp of Z. The mean of Z is X times a coefficient matrix. Extensions constrain that mean for known classes or unknown groups, and constrain Sigma to low rank or to a sparse precision." width="96%"}

Replace the gamma by a log-normal: $\mathbf{Z}_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{m}_i, \boldsymbol\Sigma)$ and $Y_{i\ell} \mid Z_{i\ell} \sim \mathrm{Poisson}\{\exp(o_{i\ell} + Z_{i\ell})\}$. The [covariance]{.mark} $\boldsymbol\Sigma$ carries the dependence between features. 📄 [Chiquet, Mariadassou and Robin](https://doi.org/10.3389/fevo.2021.588292).

::: {.notes}
The figure's $\mu$ is the mean of the latent Gaussian; here it is $\mathbf{m}_i = \mathbf{x}_i^{\top}\boldsymbol\Theta$, and $\mu$ stays $\mathbb{E}(Y \mid x)$. $o_{i\ell}$ is the offset: twice the effort adds $\log 2$. The likelihood has no closed form once $\mathbf{Z}$ is integrated out; the paper fits it by a variational approximation, in the R package `PLNmodels`. The four corners of the figure constrain either $\mathbf{m}$ (a known class, or a mixture) or $\boldsymbol\Sigma$ (low rank, or a sparse precision).

**Going further.** Aitchison and Ho (1989, *Biometrika*) give the margins: $\mathbb{E}(Y_{i\ell}) = \exp(o_{i\ell} + m_{i\ell} + \sigma_{\ell\ell}/2)$ and $\mathrm{Var}(Y_{i\ell}) = \mathbb{E}(Y_{i\ell}) + \mathbb{E}(Y_{i\ell})^2(e^{\sigma_{\ell\ell}} - 1)$, the same quadratic shape as the negative binomial with a heavier tail. The covariance of two features has the sign of $\sigma_{\ell\ell'}$, so unlike the multinomial the model allows positive correlation between counts.
:::

## A point mass of zeros is a mixture {#sec-count-zip}

A zero-inflated model is a different generative story. With probability $\pi_0$ the observation is a [structural zero]{.mark}. With probability $1-\pi_0$ it is a draw from a count distribution $f$. StatHarbor writes $\pi_0$ as $p$.

$$
\Pr(Y=0) = \pi_0 + (1-\pi_0)\,f(0),
\qquad
\Pr(Y=k>0) = (1-\pi_0)\,f(k).
$$

```{.tikz}
%%| filename: dag-zero-inflated
%%| alt: Plate diagram of a zero-inflated count over rows i: the constant pi zero gives the latent indicator Z i of a structural zero; Z i and the constant mean mu give the observed count Y i.
%%| width: 78%
\begin{tikzpicture}
\node[const] (p0) {$\pi_0$};
\node[stoch, below=9mm of p0] (z) {$Z_i$};
\node[obs, right=16mm of z] (y) {$Y_i$};
\node[const, above=9mm of y] (mu) {$\mu$};
\draw[edge] (p0) -- (z); \draw[edge] (z) -- (y); \draw[edge] (mu) -- (y);
\node[note, below=2mm of z] (n1) {$Z_i \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi_0)$};
\node[note, below=2mm of y, align=left] (n3) {$Y_i = 0$ if $Z_i = 1$\\ else $Y_i \sim f(\mu)$};
\plate{p}{(z)(y)(n1)(n3)}{$i = 1,\ldots,n$}
\end{tikzpicture}
```

A logit for $\pi_0$ plus a log-linear Poisson is the zero-inflated Poisson. The negative binomial in $f$ is the zero-inflated negative binomial. Neither is an exponential-family GLM.

::: {.notes}
StatHarbor compares a zero-inflated model with an ordinary Poisson by AIC, BIC, or a Vuong test, because those two models are not nested.

**Going further.** The zero-inflated Poisson is Lambert's (1992, *Technometrics*); it is fitted by maximum likelihood, or by EM with the latent structural-zero indicator. Vuong's test (1989, *Econometrica*) compares non-nested models through the mean and variance of the per-observation log-likelihood ratios. But the Poisson is the zero-inflated Poisson at $\pi_0 = 0$, on the boundary, so the two are in fact nested there and the Vuong reference distribution does not hold; Wilson (2015, *Economics Letters*) documents this misuse. A boundary-corrected likelihood-ratio test, or a plot of predicted against observed zero frequencies, is the safer check. A hurdle model (Mullahy, 1986, *Journal of Econometrics*) tells the other story: every zero comes from one binary process and the positives from a zero-truncated count.
:::

## A zero is an observation {#sec-zeros}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="70%"}
Sarkar and Stephens refuse the phrase "missing data" for a zero count. The picture: a minute with no cars at an intersection is a zero; an hour when the observer is away is a [missing record]{.mark}. A sequencing zero is the first of those. Imputing only the zeros treats them as holes.
:::
::: {.column width="30%"}
![](figures/generated/sketch-nongauss-b-zeros.png){.sketch-sm fig-alt="Two hand-drawn empty crossroads: on the left a green observer with a note reading 0, labelled zero; on the right an empty red stool with a note reading a question mark, labelled missing."}
:::
::::

They also drop the word "dropout" for a supposed device that writes a zero whatever the true intensity. Spike-in controls, in the papers they cite, did not support a zero-inflated *measurement* model. A zero-inflated *observation* model can still be the right margin when the latent intensity itself has a point mass at zero.

::: {.notes}
Cars-at-intersection versus absent observer—sequencing zero is the first. No impute-only-zeros; spike-in evidence against dropout measurement model. ZI on latent intensity can still be right.
:::

## Four count models, three questions {#sec-count-table}

| Model | Extra variance | Structural zeros | Exponential family |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Poisson | No | No | Yes |
| Negative binomial | Yes | No | Only if the dispersion is fixed |
| Zero-inflated Poisson | No | Yes | No |
| Zero-inflated negative binomial | Yes | Yes | No |

The practical line under the table: diagnose dispersion and extra zeros before you quote a rate ratio. An ill-matched family understates the uncertainty.

::: {.notes}
Table: extra variance, structural zeros, exponential family column. Practical line under table—diagnose before quoting a rate ratio. ZIP and ZINB are not GLMs in the strict sense.
:::

## Review of transcriptomics models {.smaller #sec-tbl-multi}

| Link $h$ | Noise on the latent scale | Methods they name |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Identity | None | NMF, scHPF |
| Identity | Gamma | NBMF |

| Neural network | Point-gamma | scVI, DCA |

Table 2. A multi-feature model writes the share through a [low-rank factorisation]{.mark} and a link $h$, then adds a noise distribution for the stochastic piece. Overdispersion relative to the Poisson measurement changes the variance of $Y$ and leaves the mean of the structured part to be read with that measurement model in mind.

::: {.notes}
Table 2: link $h$, noise on latent scale, named methods. ZINB-WaVE and scVI are multivariate—not the single-feature GLM from earlier. Overdispersion changes $Y$ variance, mean read with measurement model.
